speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. Howard C. Green (for the Prime
Minisier) moved:
That commencing on Monday. July 4, 1960, the hours of sitting will be from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.; 2 to 6 p.m. and 8 to 11 p.m. on each sitting day until the end of this session, and that the provisions of standing orders 2(1) and 6(3) be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: In view of what has happened today, Monday, June 27, I am a little diffident about speaking on this resolution. However
I	am sure hon. members of the house will realize that this was one occurrence for which the government had absolutely no responsibility.
The proposed motion will provide for several additional hours of sitting, in the first place by cutting the luncheon hour time from one and a half hours to one hour. I do not suppose anyone will quarrel very seriously with that particular change.
Then it is proposed to add one extra hour after 10 p.m. on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays. It will be recalled that frequently at this stage of the session the house sits beyond ten o'clock in the evening in any event, and I suggest that there would be no serious inconvenience to hon. members if we could make it a rule that until the end of the session the hour of adjournment should be
II	p.m. instead of 10 p.m.
Then the motion adds Wednesday and Friday evenings. Wednesday evening, throughout most of the session, is reserved for meetings of one kind or another, and there seems little reason why these could not be dispensed with in order that we may reach the end of the session that much earlier.
As for Friday evenings, I must appeal to the magnanimity or the broadmindedness of hon. members who come from Ontario and Quebec. Ever since January 14 hon. members
representing the Atlantic and western provinces have been sitting here over the week ends with time wasted in so far as the house is concerned on Friday evenings, whereas for many years Friday evenings were a most useful time for the sitting of the house and resulted in the passing of quite a large number of estimates and also brought about extremely helpful discussion.
As we all know the Friday evening sittings were taken away in order that it might be possible for hon. members living within a short distance of Ottawa to get to their homes. I realize that hon. members had good reason for wishing that change made, but I suggest that at this stage of the session it would be very helpful if the house could consider estimates on Friday evenings.
No attempt has been made to provide for sittings on Saturdays. I am not sure that this may not be necessary at a later stage, but it is certainly not included in this motion.
In drafting these proposals the government has tried to consider the best interests of hon. members and also of the staff of the house, who of course carry a greatly increased load when there are additional hours added and particularly if, for example, we were to sit right through the meal hour. That, I think, would be very unwise. I have seen it done here on one or two occasions and have had my lunch brought into the lobby for fear I might miss something that was going on. It is a very demoralizing way of carrying on the business of the house, and we are not proposing that meal times be taken away. We are also trying to consider the members of the press gallery, who have a very important function to fulfil in connection with parliament.
Hon. members will realize that there is very little legislation remaining on the order paper. On today's order paper there are three measures that have been dealt with in part, and there are three minor measures being introduced. I should really withdraw that statement; the bill of rights is one of the measures being introduced, and I would not call that a minor measure. In addition there is an act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, a bill from the other place dealing with the international boundary commission, and a resolution concerning the proposed department of forestry.
Quite good progress has been made with legislation, and it is likely that additional

speechtext:
Business of the House
progress will be made during the present week. Also, quite good progress has been made with the estimates. I am advised that by the end of the week most of the committees of the house will either have finished their actual sittings or be winding them up. Of course some of them may not have brought in final reports, but the sittings of some will be concluded although there are four or five which will have to carry on next week and perhaps some of them until the end of the session.
I ask hon. members to bear these thoughts in mind. I hope it will be possible to have this motion accepted, with the result that a great deal more work may be done commencing next Monday than would otherwise be the case.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING UNTIL END OF SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not rising to oppose the motion, but I am rising to bring to the attention of the Acting Prime Minister and the government some of the matters to which in my opinion consideration should be given on a motion such as this. When the advanced hours of sittings were considered on an earlier occasion I think we adopted the only attitude that could have been adopted at that time. A short time thereafter we have the present motion before us for additional hours of sitting. As I understand it, the effect of the motion will be to increase the hours of sitting by adding 11J hours more to our sitting time during the course of one week.
Notwithstanding what the Acting Prime Minister has said, there is no doubt but that there remain on the order paper a number of serious and contentious matters. I should like to bring these to his attention, because these additional working hours are being sought now when the order paper indicates that there is substantial work for the house to do and a considerable volume of work which, if not on the order paper, is in the hands of committees.
We are being asked to do more work, about which I am not complaining, but we are being asked to do this at a time when very important business of the session is brought down at the last minute. For instance, the combines legislation was brought down only recently and is now before a committee of the house. I understand that the committee is still waiting to hear a large number of witnesses. It is not likely that that legislation will be disposed of very quickly. The bill of rights is now on the order paper for the first time this session and this will involve a debate of some length in addition, I take it, to reference to a committee where I believe a large number of associations and groups desire to be heard. That being the

case I do not think it can be said that most of the important legislation has been disposed of. It is true that apart from the bill of rights the other bills on this morning's order paper, with possibly one exception, can be disposed of fairly rapidly.
I am sorry I cannot agree with the Acting Prime Minister's contention that there will be no serious inconvenience to those of us who sit on this side of the house because of this motion. It is not only inconvenient but difficult for those of us on this side, with these additional working hours, to have to sit on Friday evenings. My hope was that the house might find it possible to sit through the lunch hour instead of sitting on Friday evenings. The Acting Prime Minister seems to have disposed of that, because he said it would be unwise to do so. I remind the hon. gentleman that we have done it in the past not too unsuccessfully. It seems to me it is easier to work during the day time than at night. However, I realize that there may be some who are opposed to that view.
With that in mind I am wondering if the government would not give consideration to an alternative proposal. It has been the practice in the last few months to deal with legislation on Monday and Tuesday and to deal with estimates on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. The alternative proposal which I should like to make for the government's consideration-I am not going to move an amendment to this motion because I ask the government to look at my proposal before it moves as indicated on the order paper-is that on days on which legislation is being considered we sit as suggested in the motion, with an hour's adjournment during the lunch hour; because when legislation is being considered an hour sometimes gives us an opportunity to consider more carefully what should be said on the legislation which still remains on the order paper some of which is very important; and that on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, when estimates are considered, we sit through the lunch hour and adjourn at six o'clock on Friday. We would then be discussing estimates under conditions with which we have had to cope before in this house and which have not been too unsuccessful.
I suggest to the Acting Prime Minister that he give consideration to this alternative, which takes in a portion of the motion and gives to hon. members Friday evening, and of course Saturday, which this motion does not include. Therefore, in effect, the alternative proposal I make is that we accept what is now on the order paper for Monday and Tuesday, days on which legislation is generally considered, and that on the

three remaining days when estimates are considered we sit through the lunch hour instead of adopting the proposal now before the house.

I am glad to hear those cries. No party takes its duty more seriously or works harder in fulfilling it than we do. We know that the first extension of hours some three weeks ago stretched us beyond our limited resources. This motion makes our role, and we think that of the official opposition, ridiculous, and underlines the arrogance of this government in pushing the opposition around.
When electors vote in Canada they have no accurate preconception of what the makeup of the House of Commons will be, but surely they expect that there will be a function for the opposition. Hon. members recall the 1958 slogan, "Let us have another link in the Diefenbaker chain." We have 208 links in it, and now it is the missing links which beat us. We are aware that the pace for most government supporters is different from our own. We watch with envy the coming and going of the contingent out making a supplementary living at law or business, or on holiday. Between 40 and 70 are away at any one time, and the figure is even larger early in the week and at the end of the week when those fortunate fellows who live handy to the capital can junket to home and all that that means.
Those missing links defeat us. Four shifts can beat one shift at any time; and the ignominy of our position is always rubbed in. We are taunted with being repetitious, with trying to be big league and to cover everything when it is obviously beyond our means to do so. When we challenge all the rush, the forced pace of committees and the plethora of their meetings, we are told that we cannot expect to cover all such activities; that government members have some rights; that they have a job to do and wish to get it done and go home.
Then there is the more sophisticated approach to this matter. The Prime Minister,
Business of the House
with either pious reference to his recognition of the opposition's role or jaunty phrases on his love of parliament and that he is always glad to have it sitting, apparently indicates that time is not of the essence; that consideration for the opposition is centralized in his conception of parliament.

We insist that it is time the House of Commons and the government, since the government controls the House of Commons, smartened up their way of doing business. We think the best way of doing it is by splitting the session. I personally cannot see any reason why we need to be in Ottawa for more than five and a half months in the year, if we would split the session and draw up a proper schedule and get some kind of procedure actually working.
You can classify members of this house, Mr. Speaker, in a number of ways; by parties, by regions and everything else. But I always think that one of the classifications is between the commuters and the stuck. The commuters are the ones who can always get away to their homes in a comparatively short time; the stuck are those members from distant places, referred to so kindly by the minister when he introduced this motion. The pressure on the stuck is always rather severe. They are the ones who are always here on Friday afternoon and Monday, and usually they are members from a distance. They are not in the "T-to-T" school. "T-to-T" usually means Tuesday to Thursday. I could change that to "M-to-T", Montreal to Toronto. They happen to be the lucky ones. We think it is outrageous for the opposition members from the places farther away to carry the burden of the members who spend the week ends at home throughout most of the session. I notice that this morning we could almost outvote the official opposition, but this is not unusual on a Monday morning.
This party, Mr. Speaker, has the greatest respect for members of other parties who diligently attend to the business of this house in this chamber and in committees. We feel that this government by introducing motions such as this mocks us all. If it is a rubber stamp this government wants, why not sit all night, or put us on the hours reputedly worked by the Minister of Finance? Then we would be out of here in a real hurry.

speechtext: Is that an invitation?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING UNTIL END OF SESSION
speechtext:
An hon. member asks "Is that an invitation?" Certainly it is an invitation. If you want to do it this way, go ahead; you can do it.
We cannot gauge the end of the session now, Mr. Speaker. The house leader expects it to be over by mid-July. If that should happen all of us will know how cursory the examination of the work will be. The government can have its own way. The house leader and the Prime Minister certainly have the forces behind them to rub us out and push it

through, but I do not see how it can look at the business that is ahead and expect to get us out of here in two or three weeks and do any kind of a decent job. If the legislation ahead is as important as the minister argues; if the bill of rights is important; if the Combines Investigation Act amendments are important; if the changes in the Canada Shipping Act are important; if the new forestry department is important, is it not a fiasco that we should be forced to work under hours of sitting of this kind?
I suggest to the members of the government on the front benches who were in the opposition that they should have a little bit of sympathy and understanding for the fact that the opposition at the present time is not even in as good a position as they were at their weakest. At least when their numbers were smallest there were other opposition groups in the house of a little more substance in numbers. I refer to the larger C.C.F. group and the Social Credit group which, whatever you may believe of them, did carry some of the opposition load. That is not the case at the present time.
We have never had a parliament which has been so unbalanced and whose representation has been so much in favour of the government. Nevertheless it seems that the government ministers play upon the sympathies and feelings of the government backbenchers in pushing down the opposition even more than is understandable in the light of its small size. It seems to me it is time the ministry gave those in the opposition a fairer deal, because we have a difficult role to play at the present time and until the next election. It is ridiculous to think that 206 or 207 men should not have their way, but surely it is understood in a democracy that that way is best exercised by recognizing some of the rights of the minority, and these extensions of the hours of sitting are nothing more than an abuse of the minority's rights.

Mr. Speaker, it has always been my opinion that when there are such interjections as were made when I started my remarks the hon. member who has the floor should have the opportunity to reply. Most of the things I intended to say have been covered very well by the hon. member for Port Arthur but there is one thing that I think should be put on the record; that we are not alone in this country in our objection to this type of thing. To prove this I should like to refer to an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 1, 1960 and read the first two and the last paragraphs:
The British parliament is in session for the greater part of the year, and so is the United States congress. The Canadian parliament takes its duties less seriously; it gets tired, or maybe bored, after three or four months, and prepares to pack up.	,
If the Canadian parliament had spent those three or four months constructively, if in that time it had debated most or all of the important subjects, appropriations, and new pieces of legislation, it might be forgiven for getting restless around the end of May. But this is rarely, if ever, the case. Parliament crawls along for week after week fruitlessly discussing secondary issues; then it looks at the calendar, realizes how much time it has wasted, and switches into high gear. The important issues, the important legislation, are crowded into a hectic series of all-day sittings and six-day weeks, the object being to clean things up and go home by dominion day.
The last paragraph is very significant.
The imperative thing is to do away with the home stretch stampede which gives major issues hasty consideration or none at all. This is a performance which overtaxes parliament and debases parliament; which disappoints the electorate and short changes the electorate.
As the hon. member for Port Arthur said, if the Prime Minister and the government believe that the bill of rights is so important, then it should not be brought in now during the prorogation stampede. If the government does not believe that the Civil Service Act amendments-I believe there are 91 of them-are important enough to be accorded proper consideration by the house sitting during proper hours, then we certainly cannot agree with them.
It is for these reasons that we intend to vote against the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a word about the resolution and to make an appeal to the government at least to consider the alternative proposal that we put forward. From the point of view of the opposition, and I think even from the point of view of government members, I think the suggestion that we work during the lunch
Business of the House
hour in respect of estimates only has something to commend it. We have done that before. We have found that while it is perhaps inconvenient or even worse to use the lunch hour for legislation, because we do not have any time in the middle of the day to discuss matters between the morning and afternoon sessions, that objection has not applied in the past to the consideration of estimates.
Therefore we would accept the proposal, as my hon. friend pointed out, in respect of legislation, and we would hope the government would perhaps accept the proposal to work through the lunch hour in respect of estimates so we could then have Friday evening off. I think that is a reasonable proposal, and I hope the government will at least consider it. If they cannot accept this compromise this morning, perhaps they could consider it during the day and we could decide tomorrow, because the new hours of sitting will not go into effect until next week in any event, so the decision would merely be postponed until tomorrow.
I feel more strongly about this matter than I otherwise might because of the remarks of the Acting Prime Minister in connection with the legislation before us. The impression he left-and he is a very optimistic member of the house, not only in respect of our business-was that we were approaching the end and therefore we could speed up in this way because there are only a few more days to go. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that at almost the end of June the bill of rights has appeared on the order paper for the first time. That bill is going to be given a very thorough discussion on second reading and is going to be sent to a committee. There are individuals and organizations all over the country who will want to be heard and should be heard when the bill of rights goes to its committee, and that is going to take a long time.
Then we have the Combines Investigation Act, and we know what has happened before the standing committee. There are a great many organizations still to be heard. There is a great deal of interest and feeling about this bill, and it is going to take a long time before we finish consideration of this very important and controversial measure. On the order paper we also have a resolution setting up a department of forestry. Then there is also the bill to amend the Canada Elections Act, which is not yet on the order paper.
Therefore it is not a question of rushing toward an end which will be reached within a few days. The broadcasting committee has not even started its work. We have a good many weeks of work ahead of us, and I think we have to consider the extension of

Business of the House
the hours of sitting with that in mind. Therefore I hope the government will find it possible to give consideration to the compromise proposal which has been put before them. If, however, the proposal which we put forward is rejected and a vote is taken, then, because of our strong preference for our proposal but not because we object to extra hours of sitting, we will have to vote against the motion before the house at the present time. I hope that will not be necessary.
We have just heard some remarks from the C.C.F. party. While there were four members of the C.C.F. party in the house at that moment, we were told-

rise to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs upon his very reasonable and lucid explanation of a very poor case. His defence of the government and its views with respect to the hours of sitting nearly brought tears to my eyes.

We in the C.C.F. say that is not good enough.
I rise to emphasize the fact that we are protesting this procedure and will vote against this motion. I also rise to emphasize the fact that we are opposed to these unplanned sessions; and to again say that we are in favour of a split session in the future. We could then complete our work with reasonable dispatch and greater efficiency, to the advantage not only of the members of this house but of the people of Canada. When the vote is called, therefore, we will vote against the motion to emphasize our continuing protest against this unnecessary procedure. We hope also that as a result of past experience, not for the benefit of the members of the C.C.F. group in this house but for the welfare of all members, and of the country this government will learn something and improve our procedures at the next session.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DISARMAMENT-REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON RUSSIAN ACTION IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has anything which he thinks he should say to the house at this time in view of the decision taken this morning at the 10-power disarmament talks by the Soviet union, when it refused to continue to participate in the discussions that were set up as the result of agreement among the four foreign ministers, including the foreign minister of the Soviet union.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DISARMAMENT-REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON RUSSIAN ACTION IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I am afraid the 10-nation disarmament committee has been scuttled by the action of the eastern members this morning. I spoke to General Burns earlier in the morning, and apparently there were at least two western speakers on the list to participate in the discussions this morning. Mr. Zorin, the chairman of the Soviet delegation, had been told by Mr. Eaton, the chairman of the United States delegation, that there would be a western proposal submitted later this week. This was before the committee actually met.
When the committee did meet under the chairmanship today of Mr. Naszkowski of Poland, Mr. Zorin made a statement in which he accused the western members of the committee of refusing to negotiate, and made other charges, and said that the eastern members would be carrying their proposals to the United Nations. Then, in spite of the fact that western members were trying to get the floor, the Polish chairman refused to allow any of them to do so. Instead he called on each of the other four eastern members, and then he and the whole eastern delegation stalked out. Therefore no representative of the western nations was permitted to speak at all. When this happened Mr. Ormsby-Gore, the head of the British delegation, took the chair and Mr. Eaton tabled the United States plan. Of course that was all that could be done at this meeting.
I should like to explain to the house that the Soviet plan, as hon. members will recall, was issued with a great flourish of trumpets just a day or two before the 10-member committee resumed its sittings, which I think was on June 2. All the foreign ambassadors in Moscow were called in and given copies of the Soviet plan. In reporting to the house I said then that there were heavy propaganda overtones to the introduction of this Russian proposal.


Once the meetings of the committee had commenced, the western delegates endeavoured to get clarification of the various points in the eastern proposal, and made various suggestions. For example, the head of the Canadian delegation, General Burns, made a very useful speech on Friday last. I have not yet received the verbatim report of his remarks, but when I do I will probably ask for leave to table it. In addition, of course, there have been discussions going on among the four western nations concerning what reply should be made to the Soviet proposals. The Canadian reaction to the Soviet proposals was duly given to General Burns some days ago. It has been important that in the work of this committee the western nations should work together as closely as possible. Of course the eastern nations do not have that problem, because the four, apart from the Soviet, simply appear to do exactly what they are told by the Soviet.
The United States completed their reactions to the Soviet proposals late last week, and we received a copy on Thursday evening. There have been consultations in Geneva over the week end concerning the United States proposals and proposals which had been put forward by the other four western nations, including Canada, with the intent that there would be a western plan announced within the next day or two. In addition, the western plan was to have been taken before the permanent council of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization probably today or tomorrow, but certainly early this week, and then it would have been presented in the committee of ten.
I am not yet in a position to table the Canadian proposals in response to the Russian suggestions or to the United States proposals -to which, incidentally, they were very close -but in my opinion the new western proposals and the Soviet proposals of June 2, which the Soviet bloc has now refused to discuss further, could have provided a basis for detailed, businesslike and uninterrupted negotiations. It now becomes obvious that the Soviet side were not seriously interested in negotiating on the last plan they put forward. I believe that their action in stalking out of the committee as they did this morning was irresponsible, and was taken for propaganda purposes. We will now hear great talk in the United Nations general assembly about the wonderful plan the Soviets proposed, and there will be charges made that the western nations refused even to discuss it. I believe further, Mr. Speaker, that the eastern side have overplayed their hand again, just as they overplayed their hand in the breaking up of the summit conference a few weeks ago.

Canada, from the start, has been very much in earnest about the work of this disarmament committee. I believe that the Canadian government, in following that policy, has had the support of every member of the house, regardless of the party to which he or she belongs, and also the overwhelming support of the Canadian people. We shall continue to be very much in earnest and will do everything we possibly can to work out some solution to the problem. Unfortunately the problem still exists, and Canada will be willing to negotiate and, as I said, do everything she possibly can to help bring about a relaxation of tension.
Naturally these developments are a bit disturbing; but we are dealing here, I believe, with the survival of mankind. This problem we are facing is just that serious. I regret more than I can say that the Soviet and the other four members of the eastern side should have deliberately walked out of these negotiations knowing that there was a proposal to be discussed within the next day or two. Apparently they were afraid of what would be in those proposals, in so far as world public opinion is concerned. This looks like a deliberate attempt to prevent the western proposals from getting out to the nations of the world which have not been involved in the work of this committee.
I take it, of course, that there will be no opportunity now for the committee to do any further work. I understand that a message has been sent by Premier Khrushchev to the heads of government of the five western nations, but we have not actually received that. This is obviously a deliberate step taken to try to upset the west and also to gain a propaganda advantage.
I regret having to give such a report to the house, Mr. Speaker, but I am afraid that is the situation. I suggest that Canadians should not be downhearted. This is a long road that we are on now and, as I said a minute ago, it is a road which may prevent the ending of civilization. I know all Canadians will do their part in an endeavour to see that some solution is eventually found.

maintopic: DISARMAMENT-REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON RUSSIAN ACTION IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of this group wish to thank the minister for his outline of these unfortunate developments, which I know concern us all. I was going to ask the minister whether it would be possible for him to outline in brief the highlights of the western proposal. My second question is this. If this matter goes to the United Nations, as I understand is suggested by the Soviet authorities, is Canada giving consideration to putting forward proposals at the United Nations to narrow this gap and get the thing back on the rails?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DISARMAMENT-REQUEST FOR COMMENT ON RUSSIAN ACTION IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will table the western position in the house as soon as it is available, and probably also the United States reaction to the Soviet proposal and the Canadian reaction to the Soviet proposal of June 2. It is still early yet to know what course will be followed in the United Nations, but I would think it is fairly clear that the Soviet and the other four will do their best to make all the propaganda possible out of their own proposals, and that the western nations will also be dealing with their western proposals. As I said a moment ago, it now appears quite obvious that the Russian proposals were put forward on June 2 with the idea of establishing a propaganda position.

supplementary questions. In view of the fact that the external affairs committee agreed at its last session to afford the minister an opportunity, following his return from Latin America, to appear before that committee, would the minister consider that it might be useful if he would put himself at the disposal of the committee so that he, and possibly General Burns, could report in greater detail on the events which have so sadly eventuated?

Mr. Speaker, the estimates of the Department of External Affairs are set for consideration later in this week, although they may not be reached until next week. General Burns has responsibilities in Geneva for the time being, and I think it is very important that he should stay there until this whole situation is ironed out.
There was no question this morning of other western members of the 10-nation committee approving or disapproving the United States proposals. They have been under study over the week end by all five western nations, and I think the suggestions Canada has made have been accepted as alterations or additions. I do not know what attitude the United Kingdom took with regard to the proposals, but I should think that as the United States proposals are very close to our own proposals, probably the British thinking was very much like the thinking of the Canadian and United States governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I explained briefly in the debate at the resolution stage on June 21 what was the situation in this regard, and my explanation may be found at page 5229 of Hansard for that date. I should like to make it clear that I cannot accept fully the words used by my friend the hon. member for Essex East in describing the situation. I have not refused to appoint the full number asked for. Rather, it was agreed in an amicable fashion between myself and the former administration of the province that it would be acceptable if we were only to appoint three judges in the Montreal district for the time being instead of the five which the provincial legislature has authorized.
There are a number of reasons for this that were in mind during the course of discussions, and perhaps I could mention two or three of them. The first is that while there is on my part a full acceptance of the statement made by the Quebec authorities that there is an extensive backlog of cases in the Montreal district, nevertheless there are, I think, other reasons that could be advanced to explain that situation besides the simple fact of lack of judges.
I speak in this area not as an expert, but I understand, for instance, that it was the intention of the previous provincial government to appoint a commission to review the civil code of procedure, and I do not know whether that commission has been appointed as yet. It has been suggested to me that one of the reasons why there are arrears of cases is that the civil code of procedure, which has not been reviewed or revised for many years, is what I might not disrespectfully describe as a complicated and technical matter, and that a great deal of the time of the judges in Quebec is taken up in hearing applications and motions which arise under the code of procedure. It was suggested to me that a revision of that code which would result in a simplification of the rules of procedure might have the result that some of the time of the judges formerly given to hearing this type of matter might be saved, because I suppose a good deal of that type of application might be heard by what we call in the common law provinces a master in chambers.
It would seem to me that if in fact we were on the eve of a review and revision of the code of procedure which might result in a saving of the time of the judges, it would be reasonable to suggest that instead of appointing the full five we appoint three and see, first, how they got along with the three extra judges and, second, how long it might take to bring in the report and also obtain some views as to whether in fact such a report might have the result I mentioned, namely

Judges Act
the saving of the time of the judges. For those reasons it seemed a sensible and acceptable suggestion to the provincial administration that we appoint only three for the time being.
Another reason for acting deliberately in this matter instead of precipitately by appointing all five is, again, that 1 understand there is a serious problem of physical congestion in the court house in Montreal, that is with respect to rooms in which the judges may hold court. For this sort of reason and because, as I explained on the last occasion when the matter was before the committee of the whole house, the appointment of five additional judges all at one time is a very far-reaching step and one which if taken you cannot undo, it seemed to us for all those reasons it was a proper and sensible thing to suggest that instead of appointing the five at once we would appoint three as a first step and then have a look at the situation as it developed, see the extent to which these extra appointments might assist in enabling the courts to catch up with the backlog of cases, review the situation in a year's time or at the next session of parliament, and then make a final decision as to whether or not two additional judges should be appointed at that time.
I say again it is not a refusal to appoint. It is merely an agreed delay in making the full number of appointments.

Before I reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East may I deal with the last observation of the hon. member for Laurier. I assure him we will keep this matter under review and give consideration to the representations which have been made and further representations which may be made which, as he points out, come not only from the provincial authorities but also from members of the bar and of the bench, particularly in the Montreal district. That will be done between now and the next session, and we hope the experience that may be gathered in that time will afford us a satisfactory basis to answer the question as to whether or not two further appointments will be immediately necessary.
In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East, I regret that even with the best will in the world I cannot give a categorical answer as to why there is this fairly steady pressure for an increase in the number of judges; whether it is simply because of the increase in population or because of the increase in population accompanied by an increase in criminality. Of course an increase in population is inevitably one of the accompanying problems that are raised by the growth and development of the nation, and one of those accompanying factors is usually an increase in the amount of litigation. Also, as the national growth of a country increases, as that of Canada has been doing substantially and markedly over the past years, the amount and size, and if you like the importance of litigation also tends to increase and the cases become perhaps more difficult, more numerous and with weightier issues involved.

I am not suggesting for a moment that the importance of an issue is measured only in terms of the actual amount of money involved. What I am suggesting is that the type of dispute, the type of litigation that arises, does tend to become weightier with an increase in population accompanied as it has been by an increase in the national wealth of the country.
With respect to the question, or that aspect of it, dealing with criminality, the best assessment that I have been able to make is that there is not an absolute increase in criminality but that there is a proportionate increase, an increase keeping pace with the increase in population, yes, and also having a relation to the increased trend toward urbanization.
The other factor which is disturbing with regard to the increase in criminality is the increased tendency toward really shocking crimes, crimes involving the use of excessive violence. That, I think, is the disturbing element about the present figures of criminality, not so much any absolute increase in numbers as the emphasis on the particularly unpleasant types of crimes of violence. These disturbing elements are present. Certainly my hon. friend must have been aware of the concern expressed about this matter in the Montreal district in the press and elsewhere. However, in saying that I must point out that the courts for which we are providing extra judges are not exclusively courts of criminal jurisdiction. They are the superior courts of the province and have jurisdiction, therefore, in both civil and criminal matters. So that again the suggestion I make with regard to criminality and its influence on the increased work load of judges must be tempered by the fact that they are not exclusively judges of criminal jurisdiction.
Really all I can say in answer to the hon. member's question is that this request for extra judges is a trend we see all across Canada. There are frequent requests for an increase in the number of judges of superior courts and these naturally are of concern to the federal authority. It has been pointed out by hon. members opposite, and I agree, that generally speaking the federal government accepts the recommendations of the provincial government with regard to the organization of the courts because they are the governments having constitutional responsibility in that field. But I am satisfied from my review of the precedents and after discussions with my officials who also served previous administrations that my predecessors never felt their consent to such requests, should be automatic, and that they did feel that a reasonable discussion should take

Judges Act
place between the two levels of government and that the federal approach should be, as it naturally is, to suggest a minimum increase. Quite often accommodations are reached, as is the case here, between the two governments. In this case five additional judges were asked for and authorized by the provincial legislature, but it has been agreed that it will be quite acceptable that a lesser number should be appointed, at least initially. I think that sort of attitude and exchange of views is one that has prevailed when other administrations have been in office as well as now.

The representations I have received from the provincial authorities and from the bar of Montreal as well as the bench are that the present situation has been building up over several years. It is not the case that a backlog has suddenly arisen overnight but rather that the number of cases awaiting trial was becoming increasingly greater so that the provincial government felt they had to ask the legislature of the province to authorize the appointment of more judges and that the matter could not be left any longer.
I know that associate chief justice Scott of the superior court, Montreal district, has made Herculean endeavours-I do not think that is really much of an exaggeration-and in them he has been assisted by the conscientious efforts of all the puisne judges of that court, to keep pace with the volume of litigation that comes before it. They have reported to me, however, as they reported to their own provincial government, that they could no longer keep pace and that not only were they not cleaning up the existing backlog but they were not keeping pace with the number of new cases arising and being set down for hearing. Therefore this was a cumulative difficulty which required to be dealt with by the appointment of extra judges.
With regard to the reason for the extra work load, with the best will in the world I

cannot be more specific in ascribing causes than I have been in the answer I have already given, that it is a feature inevitably accompanying growth in population and an increase in national wealth.

Judges Act
overlooking the fact that this is not a revision of the Judges Act, it is an amendment. As I said on previous occasions, it is my intention ultimately to make a revision of the Judges Act when I am able to make what I regard as certain important revisions in other arrangements with regard to the judiciary and the method by which our judges are paid and the circumstances surrounding the provision for their payment. Until that time we will not be revising the Judges Act, just amending it.
If we were revising it then it would be our intention to go through it from the point of view of seeing whether there were words, phrases or sections which could be deleted so that we could come up with an entirely new Judges Act. However, for the purpose of an amendment the intention of which is to substitute one method of payment for another, namely payment of reasonable expenses instead of a per diem allowance, I do not think we should be making changes as to the headings under which the judge is entitled to be paid.
The present heading is that he is entitled to be paid his moving or transportation expenses. We do not intend to make any change with respect to that heading; the judge is still entitled to be paid under the heading of moving or transportation expenses, and therefore we decided not to make any change although we might have made a change in that wording if we had been revising the act instead of amending it. The change we made was to change the method of calculation of the payments the judge is entitled to receive from a per diem method to reimbursement of his reasonable expenses actually incurred. One of the headings under which he incurs expenses is moving or transportation.
With regard to the use of the word "reasonable" and the matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East, may I put it to him this way. You would have to have some words to ascertain what is the amount of expenses. The only other word I could think of would be "actual"-"actual travelling and other expenses". May I point out to the hon. member that in fact we would be opening the door wider to abuse by using the word "actual" than by using the word "reasonable", if there be any possibility of abuse at all. If we put the word "actual" in the statute, then a judge might spend any amount he wanted, however extravagant or unreasonable, and he would be entitled to claim it because the statute would say he is entitled to his actual expenses.

The only word I think you can use and the word which is uniformly used in statutes making provision for the reimbursement of living expenses is the word "reasonable". The judge is entitled to be reimbursed his "reasonable travelling and other expenses incurred by him in so attending".
Then the hon. member asked what is the measure of the word "reasonable". I can only say that it means reasonable having regard to the status of the judge, the circumstances of the case, the town or city in which he is sitting and where a person having the status of a judge might properly be expected to take up his quarters-the type of hotel, and so on, that he might be expected to use. It is his reasonable travelling and other expenses. I do not think the judges will have any difficulty in assessing the position or in understanding or interpreting that word. After all, one of their functions as judges is frequently to interpret and instruct juries on the problem of what "reasonable" means. When it comes to applying it to travelling or other expenses, I do not think judges will have too much difficulty in determining exactly how this applies.

speechtext:
Clause 3 is in many respects one of the most important clauses in this bill and, as I said when the minister presented the measure today, I want to make a few remarks which I regard as important. There are objections which have already been stated by those of us in the Liberal opposition earlier, particularly when we were discussing what the minister referred to the other night when he said that the bill now before the committee was a companion measure to the address which this House of Commons has approved for presentation to the parliament of the United Kingdom in respect of certain matters having to do with the district courts, the superior courts and the question of compulsory retirement of judges.
As I indicated when I spoke of these matters, and as did the Leader of the Opposition and others in this party, we are in favour of the principle of the retirement of judges at the age of 75. However, with regard to judges who have already been appointed, we feel that such compulsory retirement involves a breach of contract with the judges concerned and also that it is an interference with the independence which under our system of law all of us are anxious to see our judiciary possess.
The Ontario bar association at its meeting in February of this year expressed the view that while judges should retire at 75 such retirement should not affect those now in office, and the association passed a resolution to that effect. I mention this action taken by the Ontario bar association because the minister did refer to other resolutions passed by various bar associations including the Canadian Bar Association, resolutions which I do not believe are in conflict with the one to which I have just directed the minister's attention.
I think this is a matter of very great importance. We are now taking a step with regard to pension arrangements for judges, both those now on the bench and those to be appointed. While we do not quarrel with regard to the annuity arrangements for those to be appointed we do feel that this is a serious step to take with regard to those who are now on the bench. We say this is a breach of contract, because when those judges were appointed none of them was appointed on the understanding that there would be any interference, beyond the existing statutory ones, with his period of tenure. Thus I say that we are in favour of the annuity arrangements to the extent we have indicated. A former president of the Canadian Bar Association, Mr. Arthur Kelly, said

two years ago, we expect the judges of Canada to be independent of all pressures; we expect them to be free from any distraction which would take away their minds from onerous public duties which they have to perform, and we expect, and the public expects, that they shall maintain a standard of living which is dignified and representative of what we consider the bench represents in Canada.
In so far as the annuity arrangements are concerned I suspect that what the president of the Canadian Bar Association of that day said would be met by the provision which the minister has brought forward, but with regard to the principle of maintaining the independence of the judiciary I think by this clause we in this house are now violating a provision in a way which we should be the last ones to impose on those who by their office are called upon to adjudicate on behalf of citizens in matters affecting the law of contract. What we are doing by this measure is to ask Her Majesty to sanction a bill through her representative in this country, His Excellency the Governor General, which is in violation of a contract, though it is true the contract is not one which is enforceable in the courts but is an arrangement between the state and the appointed judges which has, nevertheless, all the elements of a contract and which otherwise would be enforceable.
We have good precedents for the position we take about this matter, and these precedents have already been mentioned. The committee has been reminded of the position taken in this regard by two former distinguished members of the bar in our country, one who later became a prime minister and the other a distinguished secretary of state. I refer to the late Lord Bennett and to Mr. Cahan both of whom vehemently opposed the initiative taken by the minister of justice in 1927 on the ground that it was an interference with the contractual arrangements, which were presumed to exist between the crown on the one hand and the judge appointed on the other. In 1930 the same minister of justice recognized the soundness of the position taken by Mr. Bennett, Mr. Cahan and others, and took steps by way of annuity arrangements to seek to meet the situation.
True the point arose again in 1933 when the arguments made by Mr. Bennett in particular were cited against the action taken by his solicitor general, Mr. Dupre. It was argued that to treat judges on the bench in the way that was contemplated and, in principle as we are doing today, was to violate a contract solemnly entered into in the only way that it is possible for the crown to enter into a contract with respect to its judges.
Judges Act
In the United Kingdom they were confronted with a situation in 1959. There they brought in a bill providing for larger pensions for the judges. It was known as the judicial pensions bill the text of which I have before me taken from an issue of the Times of November 15, 1959. By the judicial pensions bill there was a radical inroad made into the principle that no high court judge should be removed except on his own initiative by providing a compulsory retiring age of 75 with the qualification that it was to apply only to those to be appointed in the future. In other words the legislation in the United Kingdom took into account the very objection which I am making to this particular provision. I say that the annuity arrangements are satisfactory and should apply only to those who are to be appointed. The provision made for compulsory retirement of judges now on the bench should be on terms and conditions that will take into account this argument of breach of contract and also the desirability of maintaining the independence of the judiciary.
The bill passed in the United Kingdom applied, I find, to the offices of the lords of appeal, in ordinary, the lords chief justices, the master of the rolls, the president of the probate, divorce and admiralty division, the lords justices of appeal and to judges of corresponding rank in Scotland and Northern Ireland, but in every case the principle of the contractual right and the principle of maintaining the integrity and independence of the judiciary were observed.
I find it difficult to understand why the government in the face of that precedent and in the face of the attitude taken by so distinguished a right hon. gentleman of this house as Mr. Bennett, a former prime minister and president of the Canadian Bar Association and a distinguished lawyer, and others, persists in its attitude with regard to this measure in so far as existing judges are concerned. To follow the course I am suggesting, the course followed by the United Kingdom, would not add seriously to the financial obligations of the crown and I believe it would satisfy a principle which I regret is not now being observed. However, I have made this argument before and I do not want to press it except in re-stating it to indicate our concern in the matter.
While discussing this clause there are a number of other points that could be made. Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Essex East asked me to reply to the points he made in dealing with clause 3 and I think I should reply to them. They were serious points and he addressed himself to each one of the subclauses of the first part of that clause. The hon. member for Vancouver East asked me to comment particularly upon the allegation that has been made and repeated that in the proposals we have made to the house for a retirement age of 75 without providing for a continuation of full salary there is somehow a breach of contract. Perhaps I should first deal with that point briefly because it was first raised.
I must ask your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, in doing so, because, of course, this bill does not provide for a retirement age at all. The bill only provides for the payment of annuities to judges who resign their office or cease to hold their office because they reach the age of 75. It was an earlier address that provided for the retirement age and I am afraid that a renewal of the discussion which took place in the debate on that address is really out of order because this bill does not provide a retirement age for judges. All the bill does is provide for an annuity to be payable to judges who will have reached what from now on will be the retirement age of 75 years. However, Mr. Chairman, you did not interrupt my hon. friend and I did not raise a point of order. I realize that the two are closely related and I am quite prepared to meet the arguments of my hon. friends in this respect.
However, I wish to point out one thing. I wish to correct something the hon. member for Essex East said, probably inadvertently. He said that this provision, referring to the provision of annuities of two thirds of their salary at age 75, should not apply to judges who will be retired. I think what he really meant was that the retirement age of 75 should not apply to judges at present holding office. Since, however, it does apply or will apply if the address passes I am quite sure my hon. friend would then want this provision now before us to apply because without it they would not be able to get any pension at all. Indeed, under the provision now before us those judges affected by the retirement age, whether they were appointed

before or after the retirement age comes into effect, will have their pensions substantially increased over what they would have been without the bill now before us. They will get two thirds of their present salary instead of two thirds of the salary of which they were in receipt before 1955.
Therefore by this bill we are going a very considerable distance in the direction of taking care of any complaint that may be raised with respect to those judges previously appointed, namely that they suffer a financial loss. True they do not continue at full salary but they will retire on two-thirds of their present salary and I do not really think anyone should seriously suggest that is an unfair financial sacrifice, if it be one, to impose on judges.
Indeed I say that to make it possible for them to leave the bench at two thirds of their full salary is a very considerable improvement over what would be their position if we simply left them to retire when they felt like it or, alternatively, if they died while in office and their widows received a pension; because without what we are asking parliament to do today a judge would receive his pension or the widow her annuity based on the former salary and not on the present one.
However, to deal with the merits of the argument that there is a breach of contract in providing a retirement age applicable to judges who have been previously appointed, I do not want to deal at length with the matter but I should perhaps refer briefly to what I said about it before. I dealt with the question of breach of contract and I referred my hon. friends to the Reilly case which was a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in 1932, affirmed by the privy council in 1934, in which it was held that action somewhat similar to the action being taken here, taken by parliament to change the circumstances of an appointment, could not be said to involve a breach of contract.
It will be remembered that in that case the government through parliamentary action abolished an office to which somebody had been appointed. That person sued for damages for breach of contract and both the Supreme Court of Canada and the privy council then held in effect that it would be strange indeed if parliament, the legislative body which had created the office and had the power to appoint to it, could not in effect change the conditions of appointment and provide that the appointment cease without being charged with breach of contract. Here we have a case where under the British North America Act it is provided that the federal government may appoint to the position of superior court judge. Jurisdiction in that field

is vested by the British North America Act jointly in the dominion and provincial fields, the provincial legislature creating the position and the dominion authority having the power to appoint.
What we are doing now by agreement of these two legislatures, the dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures, is asking the United Kingdom parliament to amend the British North America Act so that in future the statutory provision will be that the office ceases or rather that the person ceases to hold that office when he reaches 75 so that automatically on reaching 75 there is a demission of office. This is exactly on all fours with the principle enunciated by the courts in the Reilly case. Where the legislature having competence causes to be enacted a change in the statute under which appointment is made, then, when the legislature does that there is no question whatever of a breach of contract.
May I point out that the Reilly case was decided after the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett made his criticism of the government in 1927. It is true that he alleged there was a breach of contract although he, I think, used words rather more precise than the words used by the hon. member for Essex East. But I point out to you, sir, that R. B. Bennett's criticism was voiced before the Supreme Court of Canada and the privy council had dealt with this question as they dealt with it conclusively in the Reilly case.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend permit one question? To what he says about the Reilly case I have, of course, no answer. That was a judicial decision with regard to an appointment that was not judicial. Will the minister not recognize what I said, namely that the contract which I say exists between the state and the judge is not one enforceable at law? There is no doubt about that, as I have said, but it has all the attributes of a contract, and I ask the minister whether he does not agree that all that the Reilly case says is that such a contract is not enforceable at law. It does not say that it is not a contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It went a little further than that because as I recall it, and I put the words on Hansard in the other debate, Lord Atkin in the privy council made the significant finding that under these circumstances there is not a breach of contract. He said that the contract is discharged, which he pointed out is a very different thing from a contract being breached. Whether the contract be real or implied, the situation is that the conditions are discharged by the decision of the 79951-0-343i
Judges Act
legislature which created the power to appoint and under whose joint jurisdiction the position falls.
I pointed out further on the earlier occasion that at the present time the British North America Act, the statute under which our authority arises, says that judges may be removed from office at any time by joint address of both houses of parliament. What we have asked parliament to do, therefore, is to pass an address now saying, in effect, that at age 75 all judges shall cease to hold office, which parliament has the right to do at any time. I do not accept for a moment the suggestion that there is a breach of contract, whether the contract is said to be express or implied, because it lies within the terms of the legislative authority of this parliament, having in this case the consent of the provincial legislatures which have joint jurisdiction in this field, to do exactly what we are asking parliament to do.
May I point out that there have been numerous changes made in the conditions surrounding judicial office. My hon. friends talk about a contract, express or implied. They say that a judge is entitled to assume he will continue at the salary at which he was appointed. I never heard any objections from my hon. friends when unilateral action was taken to increase the salary of judges. No question was then raised as to a contract, and there were no arguments to the effect that a judge should be prepared to carry on at the salary which attached to his office at the time of his appointment. It would of course be an absurd argument. But if one takes my friend's argument and applies it by logical extension, or if he is going to be logical about the position he has taken, then he should say that at any time there is an increase in judicial salaries the increased salary should apply only to those who are appointed subsequently and not to those previously appointed. If his argument has any merit it means that when a judge accepted office there was an implied contract that he would continue in office at the salary attached to the office at the time he was appointed. My hon. friend has never raised that argument, and of course would not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext: This is legalistic sophistry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, but if it be that it is because it is applying the argument that my hon. friend has raised. What I am doing is demonstrating the sophistry of the argument he has raised. However, I reject this argument about breach of contract altogether.
So, Mr. Chairman, I suppose it is obvious that we are not going to arrive at an od idem on this point. I am sorry that my friends

Judges Act
will not accept the force of logic. If they will not, then I am afraid there is nothing I can do about it. I am satisfied, on the basis of the research we made, on the basis of consideration that we gave to it both before and after the discussion took place in this house, that what we are doing is eminently proper and is eminently fair. We have taken account of the financial position of those who were appointed to office before the address becomes effective by making a change with respect to the pensions on which they will retire from office.
I just conclude this section of my discussion by saying that it is my strong view there must be uniformity with respect to the provisions applying to judges' salaries, with respect to the provisions applying to judges' pensions, with respect to the provisions applying to judges during the time they hold office. It would, in my view be improper to bring in legislation now which would have the effect that one group of judges on the bench could continue in office until such time as they choose to retire, while another group of judges must retire at age 75 with the pension that parliament provides. I think it would be an entirely improper thing to create that kind of distinction between judges who are serving simultaneously on the same bench. If for no other reason, therefore, it seemed to us proper to make the retiring age universal and of immediate application and to make the change in pension policy also universal and of immediate application.
My hon. friend from Essex East dealt also with the wording of subclause (b) of this proposed clause. This provides that the governor in council may grant to a judge who has continued in judicial office for at least 15 years, if he resigns his office and in the opinion of the governor in council, the resignation is conducive to the better administration of justice or is in the national interest, an annuity not exceeding two thirds of his salary. My hon. friend asks me to explain what we mean by the words "in the national interest", and why that phrase is used. He also wants to know what we mean by the words "conducive to the better administration of justice". The reason for inserting the words "in the national interest" is based on experience with at least one case that has arisen since I assumed this portfolio, and other cases which I understand arose in the past.
At the present time the existing legislation contains a provision in section 23 for the payment of an annuity to a judge who retires or resigns from office. This provision, however, is qualified by section 30 of the present act which reads as follows:

No annuity shall be granted under subsection (1) of section 23 or under section 25 unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such judge should resign his office.
In other words, the only condition under which an annuity may now be paid to a judge who resigns other than by reason of sickness is, if in the opinion of the governor in council, the resignation is in the public interest. It has been my experience, and I believe that of my predecessors, that this provision is difficult of interpretation and application.
Let me refer to a hypothetical case in order to avoid identification, actual or potential. Let us suppose that a judge is appointed to a position, not by the federal authority but by some other authority, either public or private, and by whom it is then said to the federal government, we consider that the assumption by this judge of this alternative employment is very much in the public interest. This might be alleged and argued with considerable vehemence. It might be alleged and argued that the federal government which took the position this was not in the public interest, in the sense the words are used in the act, was being selfish and narrow.
But, Mr. Chairman, it does seem to me that when you are dealing with federal legislation and dealing with positions for which parliament provides the salaries and the annuities those words "in the public interest" should be interpreted as meaning the public interest in the sense of the national or federal aspect of the public interest. There have been cases, it is quite true, where former governments have appointed judges to offices within the disposition of the dominion government, such as ambassadors. I can think of at least one, if not more cases in this category. In those cases, the opinion was that the judge's resignation of his office in order to accept the appointment was in the public interest. It was represented in one or two cases that this was a higher or more important calling to which he was being appointed. I think there is no difficulty with the basis of that interpretation because it was an appointment by the national authority. The difficulty arises where you have the situation where the judge himself desires to go to another appointment or some other body wishes to obtain his services in some other capacity, and it is then represented that this resignation in order to enable the appointment to take place is in the public interest.
There has been misunderstanding and difficulty occasioned by this situation in the past. As I say, in my view the application to be given to the these words "is in the

public interest", is in the field for which the federal government is responsible, and we are therefore changing the words of the statute in this case to make it clear, or as clear as we can make it, that the consideration to be borne in mind is the interest within the jurisdiction, authority and control of the federal government and parliament. That is the reason for the use of the words "is in the national interest". We are using the word "national" instead of the word "public".

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister think that he has dealt sufficiently with the phrases-

speechtext:
No, I am coming to that now; it is another part of the problem which was raised.
The reason for the use of the words "is conducive to the better administration of justice" is closely related to the problem I have just been discussing. At the present time the only way in which an annuity can be paid to a judge who resigns his office under section 23 is either if infirmity or sickness disable him from discharging his office, or if he is resigning for some other reason, and in the opinion of the governor in council it is in the public interest that he should resign his office.
When you come to apply this to the case of a judge who has served 15 years or more and who may have reached the point really where his energy and ability on the bench have in fact been exhausted but you really cannot say he has such sickness or infirmity as to disable him from discharging his office, then it seems to us to be pretty harsh for the governor in council to have to say, "Yes, your resignation will be accepted and your annuity can be paid because it is in the public interest that you should resign".

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I agree with that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext: The reason why we use the words "is conducive to the better administration of justice" is to cover exactly that type of case.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext: What about a judge whose conduct is in question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I come to that in a moment; I will just complete what I was saying on this point.
In other words, this will furnish a way in which we can pay an annuity without having to go so far as to say, "It is in the public interest that you should resign your office", and actually make that as a finding of the governor in council. We can now simply say, "Yes, we agree, under all the circumstances that conditions are such that it would
Judges Act
be conducive to the better administration of justice if you wish to resign"; and in that case an annuity can be paid.
It is perfectly true that this would also cover the case of a judge whose conduct was in question, although perhaps not misconduct of such magnitude as to warrant the submission of an address or the appointment of a commission of inquiry. Those two courses, after all, are both very far-reaching and rather terrible steps to have to take, and would only be taken in what I might call extreme cases. But there are lesser cases where a judge's conduct might have been called in question and it is perhaps his feeling that he himself has come to the conclusion that the administration of justice would be better served if he resigned. By the use of these words in the statute he could resign if he had served 15 years under circumstances where it was deemed to be conducive to the better administration of justice and he would be entitled to his full pension.
Where a judge had given faithful or valuable service for 15 or more years there is no reason why he should not be allowed to submit his resignation under such circumstances and receive his full annuity. Indeed, being practical about it, I think it is a sensible step to make this provision, because if you did not provide some such way in which he could resign and receive his annuity it would be extremely unlikely that you would get his resignation in any event. As I have said, it is rarely, if ever, that one would use the terrible provision I have mentioned which is the only other way that a judge can be removed from the bench.
The third provision which the hon. member asked me to discuss was that contained in clause 23 (1) (c), which reads;
(c) a judge who has become afflicted with some permanent infirmity disabling him from the due execution of his office, if he resigns his office or by reason of such infirmity is removed from officein that case the governor in council may grant to such judge an annuity not exceeding two thirds of his salary.
The hon. member raised the question in that connection as to whether there should not be some provision providing for a minimum term of service before a judge who resigned his office by reason of sickness or infirmity still could receive full pension. May I point out to the hon. member that the present law provides exactly what we are providing here, namely section 23 (1) of the present Judges Act which is as follows:
The governor in council may grant to a judge of a superior court who has continued in office as such for at least 15 years or is afflicted with some

Judges Act
permanent infirmity disabling him from the due execution of his office ... an annuity not exceeding two thirds of-
-his salary. We are making no change in this regard, and I think that is proper because I do not think a judge who in good faith makes all these changes and sacrifices required of him, disposes of his practice and office and who makes other far-reaching financial arrangements in order to accept an appointment to the bench, who is then stricken unexpectedly with some sickness disabling him from discharging his duties, should be deprived of his right to an annuity if he resigns on account of that disability.
The final provision which the hon. member asked me to comment on-

-was with respect to (1) (d). The hon. member says he is now satisfied with that and I am glad to hear that. However, there is one aspect of it which I might point out, and that is that at the present time the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, the exchequer court and the territorial courts in Canada have to serve a minimum of ten years before they are entitled to a pension. We are simply extending that in effect to judges of superior and county courts by providing that future appointees must have served ten years in order to be entitled to full pension on reaching the retirement age of 75.
I think the implications will be obvious and I think they are proper. If we are providing a retirement age universally of 75 years, then I think it is quite proper to provide in effect that you must not appoint anyone over 65 to that office if he is to receive the full pension. There is no prohibition against appointment; it is merely a provision that he must have served ten years in order to retire on full pension at 75, and the assumption is that there will not be very many appointments over the age of 65. That is already the case in the highest court in the land and we see no reason for not extending it to other courts.
