speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of remarks to make on this. I am not a lawyer but I am quite interested in this matter.
About a year ago on the department's estimates I asked the minister whether the government was contemplating legislation along this line. The minister said he was working on it and hoped to make an agreement with the provinces shortly. He has worked very fast in one year in order to reach agreement with all the provinces.

I have made a few fast calculations with respect to the annuities proposed for judges of county and district courts. Those receiving a salary of $10,000 were formerly entitled to a pension of $5,333 which will now be increased to $7,000, an increase of 30 per cent. Puisne judges and judges of all provincial and federal courts formerly receiving a pension of, say, $9,600 will now receive $11,266, or an increase of 17 per cent. The percentages will vary, of course. I think this represents a very substantial increase in what might be called the over-all pay, or emoluments, of judges. When a vacancy occurs on the bench the minister of justice and his officials must, of course, look for the best person to fill that vacancy and the proposals which are now being put forward will serve as an extra inducement.
I should like the minister to comment on one point and tell us whether he thinks we are likely now to have a reservoir of trained judges who will be available to act on royal commissions and boards of inquiry thus leaving the serving judges free to do the work for which they were appointed, namely to take care of the courts. I think that perhaps the increase in the number of judges is not unconnected with the fact that some of our judges are doing too much outside work. It may be that because of the extra fees, the extra income, that such work has been regarded by the judges with a favourable eye. I think we should discourage this practice and try to keep our judges working on the job they were appointed to do. The present salaries are, in my opinion, adequate. They may not be anywhere near the sums which the judges were making when they were at the bar, but they are certainly adequate, particularly in the light of the changes made in this present bill. I think we can expect that our judges should stick to the bench and keep away from outside activity, no matter how financially rewarding such activities might be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house for second' reading is undoubtedly a very important one. It is important for the effects it has on large numbers of employees in the public service and important in principle but when we examine it we find it deals with different isolated points in existing legislation which I think the house generally will agree is very good legislation. That being the nature of the bill before us it raises some question as to getting the best possible legislation out of this bill by debate at this stage.
It strikes me that if one were to seek to debate a great many questions of principle affecting the subject of the superannuation of public servants no valid result will be obtained. While it is technically possible to do so under the rules-the bill being in such language-in this particular instance it is probably not desirable to do so. I believe the points dealt with in the bill can be more adequately examined in the special committee to be set up for the purpose of dealing with this legislation to which committee the bill


will be referred following second reading. In the committee questions can be directed to the minister and the appropriate officials of the department having to do with the administration of the fund. Questions may be put to the actuarial authorities in the minister's department and others who may want to be present. By following the procedure outlined by the minister of giving the bill second reading now and having it referred to the special committee, when it comes back into the house if there are any questions still unanswered there will be an opportunity in the committee of the whole to discuss the points on particular clauses. I think that is a desirable course to follow on the whole.
There is one point concerning which I should like some information from the minister. If he has it readily available he may give it to the house when he replies or, if not, it could be given in committee. I refer to the whole question raised by the amendment changing the rate of contribution. I have in my hand sessional paper No. 60-B entitled "Report on actuarial examination of the superannuation account in the consolidated revenue fund as at December 31, 1957" tabled in the house on Monday, June 20, 1960. Two paragraphs which squarely deal with this point are found on page 24 of that return. The first reads as follows:
1.	The estimated deficit in the superannuation account as at December 31, 1957, was $137.7 million. It is recommended that this deficit, together with the "unamortized portion of actuarial deficiency in the superannuation account," amounting to $139 million, be liquidated as soon as may reasonably be possible. It is also recommended that, until liquidation of the deficit has been completed, interest be credited to the account in respect of the amount of deficit remaining from time to time, to keep it from growing with interest.
The second paragraph reads in part as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PILOTS AND PILOTAGE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-80, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement an arrangement with the government of the United States to coordinate the control of marine pilotage on the great lakes in the interests of safety.
The existing part VI of the Canada Shipping Act governs marine pilotage in general. However, many of the provisions of this part are not suitable for application on the great lakes where ships must cross and recross the international boundary many times during the course of a voyage. Further, one of the main features of Part VI is that acceptance of pilotage services is optional, although in some districts the payment of pilotage dues is made compulsory whether or not a pilot is employed.
On the great lakes we have large bodies of water and connecting rivers which until the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway were cut off from the sea except for comparatively small vssels. Over the years a specialized practice of navigation has grown up in these waters. They have their own collision regulations which are different in some respects from the regulations for preventing collisions at sea. Again the operators of lake ships, both Canadian and United States, used a common language which facilitated communication by radiotelephone. In fact, the use of the radiotelephone became so common on the great lakes that practices were laid down by intergovernmental treaty and the use of
Canada Shipping Act
voice communication between ships became an added safeguard in the avoidance of collision.
Before the opening of the seaway the number of ocean ships which entered the great lakes was comparatively small, as were the ships themselves. Their masters and officers were experienced and, where necessary, they employed local mariners to assist them. With the opening of the seaway large ocean ships entered the great lakes in considerable numbers and competent pilots were required to navigate them, particularly through the restricted portions of those waters. The need for some official control was evident and early in 1959 my department organized a staff of government employed pilots for assignment on request as pilots for the waters lying between Port Weller at the lake Ontario end of the Welland canal and Sarnia at the lake Huron end of the St. Clair river. The international portion of the St. Lawrence river from St. Regis or Cornwall to lake Ontario was already provided for, as far as the availability of pilots was concerned, by an existing pilotage district.
The Canadian attitude toward pilotage, as reflected in existing law, has been that the safety of the ship is the responsibility of the master of that ship. A prudent master invariably employs a pilot when pilots are available for the navigation of waters with which he himself is not familiar, but the responsibility is his to decide whether or not he requires a pilot. In the United States, on the other hand, the employment of pilots in ports and other restricted waters has been compulsory. This attitude was reflected in an earlier proposal from some United States sources to make pilotage compulsory in all the United States waters of the great lakes basin including the United States portions of the river St. Lawrence. In view of the congestion of traffic in the connecting waters of the great lakes, we recognized the desirability of departing from our traditional attitude and agreed to collaborate with the United States government in making pilotage compulsory in these waters. However, we did not feel that the employment of local pilots was essential from a safety point of view while the ships were on the open waters of the great lakes.
The United States administration has, as a result of our discussions with them and their own study, decided that the requirements of safety would be met if among the ships' officers there is one who has had some experience of the great lakes and has by examination established that he is familiar with the great lakes rules and has an adequate

Canada Shipping Act
knowledge of the English language. Congress has passed legislation to give effect to this decision.
Our bill is intended to provide the machinery whereby we can complement, in the Canadian waters of the great lakes, the provisions of the new United States legislation and regulations which may be made thereunder. We propose to do this by a new part VI-A of the Canada Shipping Act which will deal only with great lakes pilotage. We are thus leaving undisturbed, except for one small item, the existing pilotage provisions of part VI. This one exception is an additional section 356A which will provide, pursuant to a reciprocal arrangement, that in the case of a pilotage district made under part VI and which forms part of the great lakes basin a United States pilot may act as such without violating Canadian law.
The proposed Part VI-A starts by defining the terms "designated waters", "great lakes basin" and "registered pilot". I would draw to your attention that the wholly Canadian part of the St. Lawrence river east of St. Regis on the south side of the river opposite Cornwall is not affected by this legislation.
Section 375B is what might be termed the operative section of this bill. I should add, in parentheses, at this point that both Canadian and United States lakers will be exempted from these pilotage requirements. This section provides that no vessel of 250 gross tons or over shall be operated:
(a)	in designated waters unless it is being piloted by a registered pilot; or
(b)	in undesignated waters of the great lakes basin unless there is on board a registered pilot or an officer having the qualifications prescribed by regulation.
In practice the "designated" waters will we expect, be the river St. Lawrence from St. Regis west, the Welland canal, the waters joining lake Erie and lake Huron and those joining lake Huron and lake Superior. However, it will be possible for the President of the United States to designate other waters on the United States side, including perhaps certain ports or other congested areas, and for the governor in council to do likewise on the Canadian side if experience shows such action to be desirable. The undesignated waters will, in general be the open waters of the great lakes. Here an ocean ship will be navigated by her own master and officers, but unless one of them possesses certain qualifications prescribed by order in council there must be on board and available for call a registered pilot.
As stated in an aide memoire which was tabled on February 23, 1960, the qualifications which will be required of the master or one of the officers of a ship which may

navigate the open waters without a registered pilot being on board, as presently contemplated, will be:
(1)	possession of a master's certificate of competency valid for voyages in any part of the world;
(2)	experience of at least two round trips within the preceding two years in the open or undesignated waters where the vessel will be operating;
(3)	a working knowledge, as evidenced by examination, of the great lakes rules of the road;
(4)	proficiency in the English language sufficient to make effective use of the radiotelephone;
(5)	a knowledge of the practice of following separate courses on the great lakes, giving due regard to the suitability of such courses for deep draft vessels.
I might say that the certificate of competency which I have just described we propose to designate as "Great lakes-open water navigation certificate".
Section 375B also contains a clause providing for the exemption by the Minister of Transport of any ships from the above requirements. This clause will make it possible for the Minister of Transport to exempt regular lake vessels, both United States and Canadian, which obviously have no need of this requirement. There is also a clause to ensure the possibility of continued movement of vessels without violation of law when no registered pilots are available or in extraordinary circumstances which make it necessary for the master to avail himself of the best assistance that can be found at the time.
Section 375C sets out the powers of the governor in council in making regulations under this part. These provisions will enable us to make adjustments as experience may dictate and as may become desirable during consultations with our United States counterparts. As will be seen, the power to make regulations includes the designation of the waters in which registered pilots will be required; prescribing qualifications of a Canadian registered pilot and those required by a ship's officer to enable his ship to proceed without a registered pilot in the open waters; and also the fixing of fees to be charged for examinations and for the services rendered by Canadian registered pilots.
Subsection 2 of this section provides that the Minister of Transport may fix the number of Canadian pilots that may ge registered under this part. This is necessary because United States pilots are entitled to a fair share of the work and both sides have agreed to control the number of pilots in this manner.
The remaining provisions cover penalties for violations and provide that the act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation.
All these provisions are expressed or implied in the United States bill which is necessarily longer than our bill because of their

different legislative system. We believe that our proposed bill will enable us to work in co-operation with the United States authorities in establishing a safe, controlled and efficient pilotage system on the great lakes.
The United States bill will not come into force until four months after the issuance of regulations made pursuant to it. Before such regulations are made we expect that there will be further discussions between Canadian and United States officials so that the regulations on either side will have substantially the same effect.
Our bill will not be proclaimed until working regulations satisfactory to both sides have been formulated. The date of proclamation should coincide with the effective date on the United States side which is likely to be prior to the opening of the 1961 season of navigation.
Following my usual practice, I propose to refer this bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the measure which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) discussed prior to the adjournment at six o'clock is an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, which is of importance not only because of the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway but because of its effect on those in the great lakes area. It is also of importance to the house in general.
The main features of this legislation are somewhat different from those which were envisaged last year. At that time the minister brought before the house a bill which we on this side said we thought was premature in that an agreement had not then been reached between Canada and the United States concerning the matters that were then up for discussion between the two countries. As the minister stated earlier, there was no necessity for this kind of legislation prior to the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway but because of the seaway and for other reasons as well it became necessary to enter into discussions with the United States to ascertain if the minds of both countries were ad idem so far as pilotage is concerned. One important reason was the increase in the number of ships that moved inland between the lakes and Canadian ports-that is,
Canada Shipping Act
domestic traffic-as well as ocean-going ships that moved from points on the continent of Europe and elsewhere to the inland waters of the great lakes-St. Lawrence basin.
As I have pointed out, it then became necessary to enter into discussions with the United States. When the matter was up for discussion last year I suggested to the minister and to the government that they should give consideration to the establishment of a committee on pilotage as was done with respect to the committee on tolls established for the seaway. In the case of the tolls, as the house knows, it was a matter which was quite successful. An international committee composed of I have forgotten how many Canadians and how many United States citizens-I think three on each side-after consultation with each other was able to establish a tariff of tolls and then, following consultation, had those tolls submitted to the public following hearings that took place in both Canada and the United States.
It seemed to me that if something akin thereto was followed by both countries in so far as pilotage was concerned it would be extremely helpful. While that may not have been followed to the letter I think there was a committee from the Department of Transport which dealt with an opposite committee in the United States composed of members of the coastguard and other such services.
I know that at one time the United States held very strong views with regard to pilotage because they had had some experience on the Panama canal. I think they would have liked Canada to follow the same practice on the Welland canal and in the great lakes area as was followed there. At the time the matter was up for discussion last year I made this statement which can be found at page 2337 of Hansard of April 7 1959:
It seems to me that we should not be asked to pass this kind of legislation until we know what the legislation in the United States congress is going to be. Last year there was a bill brought before congress: it did not go through. We know what the nature of that bill is; I have a copy of it here in my file. But the bill which is now before the United States congress, even if it does go through all of its stages, cannot possibly be passed until October or November of this year. So I ask the question: Are we being asked to pass this kind of legislation before we know what the concurrent legislation on the other side is likely to be? The minister a moment ago used the expression "reciprocal legislation". Well, this is not reciprocal legislation. It is unilateral legislation. It cannot be reciprocal legislation until the two parties have agreed to what they want in the legislation.
After a plea which I made at that time giving additional reasons why the bill should not be discussed at that time the minister very kindly decided to withdraw the bill and

Canada Shipping Act
enter into discussions with the United States with a view to reaching an agreement. Therefore the objections which we on this side of the house might have had to the bill last year no longer exist at this time in so far as this is concerned. I take it now that in effect an agreement has been reached between Canada and the United States on the subject of pilotage on the great lakes and I presume we will have the benefit of the evidence before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to analyse what transpired during the course of these negotiations.
The part to which I had reference and which came before the United States congress last year and which had not been passed at that time, in fact which lapsed and died with the prorogation of the United States congress, has now been removed. I believe this year it has been approved or is about to pass the last stage of congress. Therefore,
I repeat, the objections which were raised to this kind of legislation no longer obtain at this time.
There are two other matters that should be discussed. One is that the bill no longer contains those amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which were envisaged last year and which meant in effect the abolition of the pilotage districts of Montreal and Quebec. I commend the minister on having taken those clauses out of the bill. I think it would have been a mistake to abolish those districts which have been in existence now for close to 200 years, where pilots rely on navigation for their living and where over those many, many years the trade or profession of pilot has been handed down from father to son through many generations. I will not spend any time dealing with that but I think the government and the minister were well advised to withdraw those clauses which I thought at that time were objectionable.
We are now left with a part which deals exclusively with pilotage on the great lakes, and it is to known as part VI-A. It is rather difficult to comment upon the terms of this bill which, as Your Honour knows, appeared on the order paper for first reading the first time this morning and which we consented to allow to receive its second reading so that it could be discussed and then sent on to committee. It is rather difficult I say, to comment on the various clauses without having read the bill more carefully. It is not impossible but it is rather difficult to deal seriatim with the clauses which are before us. I have no intention of doing that.
During the dinner recess I had an opportunity to read the statement made by the minister earlier and I think I should like to leave the matter in this way. Since the

bill will be sent to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, it will be possible there to hear the evidence of the departmental officers and I presume also the evidence of anyone else who may feel affected or aggrieved or, in fact, helped by this legislation. I do hope the minister will not call the meeting too soon so that it will be possible for those who are interested in the bill to make the representations they desire to make.
In the course of his remarks the minister said nothing about the attitude of the pilots toward this legislation. In his reply perhaps he would make some reference to that. What is the attitude of the pilots in the Montreal-Ottawa-Kingston area? What is the attitude of the pilots which were established by the department in order to meet a situation which was aggravated by certain circumstances which were discussed in the house last year? What is the attitude of the pilots who will be operating in the restricted area and the designated waters under the terms of authorization by appointment through the governor in council? There have been no indications of any attitude in so far as they are concerned.
I ask these questions because last year there was considerable agitation in all fields of navigation with respect to this legislation. There was agitation among pilots in the areas extending all the way from the lower St. Lawrence right up to the head of the lakes. Representations were made by the shipping federation of Canada and also by various other groups. That is why I think the minister is well advised to send this legislation to a committee. In the committee we should find out what are the views of those various associations. There we shall have an opportunity to study the bill more carefully. I also think we should get some indication of the effect of this legislation either from our own officers in the Department of Transport or from witnesses from other places.
I do not know whether the minister has given any consideration to calling witnesses from the United States to indicate the necessity for the first clause and a subsequent clause of the bill. I do not know that when the United States legislation was brought before congress Canadian witnesses gave evidence. In fact, I think it was Canada which was responsible to a large extent for getting the United States to change its attitude on this legislation. If I remember well, the state department, the St. Lawrence seaway corporation, the United States entity which built the United States share of the seaway, and the department of commerce were all favourable

to the Canadian point of view. I think it was only the United States coastguard which held strongly to the view that the pilotage should apply to all of the great lakes areas, both restricted an open waters as well, and it was the Canadian group which was successful in getting the United States, in large part at least, to amend their views in that respect.
Perhaps I have said more than I intended to say at this time but I leave the matter with this final word. It seems to me that the first thing we should want to know about in committee and be apprised of in this house for further discussion when the bill comes up in committee of the whole is the kind of agreement which was reached with the United States.
I am pleased that the designated areas have been indicated already by the minister, so that we know now that those areas are in conformity with the views which were held by Canada during the time of the negotiations with the United States.
So, without saying more, I resume my seat confident that when we have the various witnesses before the committee we will then be able to get not only a better idea of this legislation but will also be able to ascertain what in effect will be its result upon pilotage in the great lakes-St. Lawrence basin.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PILOTS AND PILOTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will not keep the minister long. We know he is anxious to go out and get the good word from New Brunswick. When the bill was originally brought in a year ago we thought it was a bad bill and the evidence which was brought out in the Senate committee which investigated the matter last year was tending to substantiate this view when the minister, as a result of the request of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier), which I would have made had I had the opportunity to make it, withdrew the bill. We now have a much simpler and more clear-cut bill. On the face of it we are for it and it only remains to be seen what the detailed information will be in the committee.
I think it is worth making one background statement, Mr. Speaker. The reason I originally became concerned about this matter was through the great lakes pilots association, a group which was in effect, in their terms anyway, locked out by the shipping federation of Canada. It was a type of union, although the classification of the great lakes pilots association as a union brought some disagreement. Two summers ago we had in effect a lockout or strike on the lakes and
Canada Shipping Act
the great lakes pilots association took vigorous exception to the action of the Department of Transport in failing to back them up or to require the shipping federation of Canada to act in a certain way.
There were fears expressed, largely as a result of statements by the United States C.I.O. unions that control pilotage on the United States side, that pilotage on the great lakes was going to become a wonderful example of featherbedding. There were pictures of three pilots on a large foreign ship being paid at the rate of approximately $85 a day, and naturally shipping interests both in Canada and the United States became quite concerned about this. I might say that the Canadian pilots in the great lakes pilots association also became concerned about this picture of the kind of ramp that the Americans were planning.
Last year the government, in order to head off any difficulties, made the pilots temporary civil servants and now that the minister-I remind him again that he is a great socializer-has the Canadian pilots on the great lakes in the government service it looks as though this is going to become a permanent arrangement. The stumbling block with respect to legislation last year in relation to the Americans really lay with Admiral Richmond, the head of the United States coastguard service. Admiral Richmond was strongly against the Canadian arrangement because he thought it was not strict enough in its requirements as to competence and that giving Canadians the power to give a temporary licence to foreign masters who came to Montreal and were proceeding thence up the great lakes would open the United States parts of the lakes to grave dangers.
I have a copy of the report of the United States senate committee on interstate and foreign commerce with respect to bill S.3019 which is the United States counterpart of the bill before us. It was reported out of the committee several weeks ago and I think it is of interest to have a brief review from the report. It reads in part as follows:
Opening of the St. Lawrence seaway in 1959 has greatly complicated vessel safety problems on the great lakes by making possible entry into the lakes of ocean vessels of higher tonnage and in far larger numbers than previously was the case. In addition to the 2,206 United States and Canadian vessels operating on the lakes exclusively or in large part, some 1,033 foreign commercial vessels and 61 vessels under U.S. registry made round voyages on the lakes in 1959. All indications are that this total, of foreign vessels particularly, will increase in the years ahead.
This is the interesting point in view of Admiral Richmond's objections of last year.
The upsurge of foreign vessels navigating U.S. waters of the great lakes, and the entry of U.S. ocean vessels into the area, present a definite

Canada Shipping Act
threat to safe navigation. There is presently statutory requirement for the use of qualified pilots on both U.S. and Canadian vessels navigating only on the lakes. However, operation of the oceangoing vessels, without skilled lake pilots, as evidenced by the reported accidents and near accidents during the first year's operation of the St. Lawrence seaway, presents a threat of considerable magnitude not only to the lake vessels, but also to the ocean vessels whose officers, in some cases, may not be sufficiently familiar with the great lakes rules of the road, the restricted waters, etc.
The report goes on to set out the reasons why the senate passed this bill, indicating, for example, that the shipping federation of Canada has approved it. I would construe that these paragraphs emphasizing the dangers of foreign shipping are really evidence that the Canadians, through the minister's department, must have made compromises with the Americans. It is very difficult for us to see the compromises because the bill is still in skeleton form. The interesting point that was made in both the senate and house of representatives committees in the United States was that the United States merchant marine institute and the United States pilots, as I understand it, asked that the powers as to establishing various areas and the requirement be left with congress rather than with the executive branch. This problem is examined' in the report of the senate committee and it is felt that in order to have any kind of decent co-operation with the committee the executive must be in charge of the regulations in the United States.
Therefore we have a situation where the United States congress has in respect given over control in this particular matter to the executive, working through the commerce department which will handle the licensing of pilots, and the coastguard which will judge their competence. If we follow the congressional system, this is a concession on the part of congress and indicates that they are putting a great deal of faith in the negotiations and the arrangements to come with the Canadians.
But in the bill we have before us in this house we have very few details. I missed the minister's statement as to just what areas are going to be designated as restricted areas for pilotage but I am very curious and will expect details in the committee in order to know what the situation is going to be in the St. Mary's river, lakehead and Duluth areas because this bill, this report-I must not give the impression it is a bill-from the United States senate committee indicates that they expect the St. Mary's river will be a restricted area.

That generally conforms with what the Americans expected. So it appears that the relationships after the passing of this bill, given the passing of it, depend completely so far as their amicable future is concerned upon negotiations between the Department of Transport and the United States department of commerce. We expect that this will not necessarily be easy because the Americans have an added pressure under which the minister's department does not operate.
The United States, as I pointed out to the minister before, believes in free enterprise and in trying to push it as far as possible. They are not creating a situation in which their pilots become civil servants, as the minister has done, because these pilots in the United States are organized in unions. Operating on this free enterprise basis they are always going to be, I would judge, pressing forward complaints about the ratio of pilotage as between Canadian pilots and United States pilots. As the minister knows, there have already been complaints from the New York and Ohio pilots. This indicates to me that we must expect to hear in committee what kind of continuing system is planned in order to keep this relationship balanced as fairly as possible. It would seem to me we need some kind of continuing small committee perhaps, composed of representatives from each side and a third party as a referee or arbitrator. I do not believe we should kid ourselves that this arrangement is going to work smoothly and automatically once it is passed.
At any rate, the point I wanted to make in connection with this bill which is still not crystal clear-here again we have to wait for the regulations-is what is going to be the position of the foreign masters? This is a sensitive point in so far as the United States pilots are concerned. I can only offer the minister the benefit of the experience we have had in our particular area as a result of talking to people on tugs around the elevators. They are in general agreement that the foreign "salties" as they are called are not nearly as capably handled as the lake ships. This is not because the foreign masters are not as

good as the lake masters but because of exceptional difficulties within the great lakes system and the fact these ocean ships have a higher freeboard and do not have the handy winches and controls that the lake ships have. I would suggest to the minister that he make sure when the regulations are drawn up that very tight control is kept on the giving of licences of any kind to foreign masters.
I believe he needs especially, since the United States is not going to have this right to award licences which the minister's officials are going to have, to safeguard his responsibility to make sure that the licences of Canadian pilots are respected. I hope, for that reason, he will make sure that the level of competence required from foreign masters is of such a degree that it will not demean in any way the certificates or licences that Canadian pilots hold.
I would hope also that the minister will be prepared in committee to give us some idea as to whether he plans to make this pilotage service a permanent part of his department by bringing it fully under the requirements of the Civil Service Act. I believe this about sums up the points I wanted to make in connection with this particular bill. I reiterate that we support it. We hope to hear more about it and in general our views are quite compatible with those expressed by the hon. member for Laurier. We think it is a marked improvement over what the minister presented formerly.

I do not intend to say very much at this time regarding this bill. However, I should like to say that I approve, in principle, the passage of such a measure. I am looking forward to having a good look at the bill and hearing it discussed in committee. I should like also to commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) for the manner in which he has moved into this problem of pilotage on the great lakes which two years ago was in quite a muddle. Last year he took the first step which was to put the pilots more or less under the civil service by having them paid by the department. I feel that was an excellent move.
When the bill was first considered I was of the opinion that perhaps pilots should be required all the way through the great lakes. However, I believe that the way the bill is presently framed whereby it will not be necessary to have first class pilots on the open lakes but certificates to be issued to navigators, solves the problem. I feel this provision will be reasonably satisfactory to the pilots themselves.
In so far as the pilots themselves are concerned, I think they will approve of the fact it
Canada Shipping Act
is not going to be the policy of the government to require class B or second class pilots on the open waters; that was something that the pilots did not like. I believe this new set-up under which certificates will be issued will more or less solve the problem.
As I said at the beginning, there is not too much we can say about the bill now. I am certainly going to look forward to hearing the bill discussed in committee.

Mr. Speaker, the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway has made changes in the shipping act imperative. With the advent of the St. Lawrence seaway we have had a demonstration of its value through the number of ships which have used this great highway of commerce during its first year of operation. The result has been that the lakehead port cities of Fort William and Port Arthur, for example, have been brought to second place in terms of tonnage. The port of Montreal shipped 17,985,975 tons; the lakehead shipped 12,900,000 tons; Vancouver gained third place with 11,845,810 tons; Hamilton was fourth with 7,488,850 tons and Toronto was fifth with only 4,798,435 tons.
I am advised that already this year 60 ocean freighters have docked at the lake-head which represents about half of last year's total. This augurs well for a substantial increase in shipping tonnage in 1960, and eventually the lakehead might overtake even the great port of Montreal. During the 1959 season there were 2,120 arrivals at the lakehead. It is, therefore, only reasonable to expect that the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur will request that the lakehead harbour be given the status of an ocean port. I ask the minister that the request of the joint transportation committee of the Fort William-Port Arthur chamber of commerce and the lakehead port association be given serious consideration.
We are pleased with the government's decision to proceed with the construction of the seaway terminal.

Mr. Speaker, during the 1959 session of parliament, in anticipation that a change in the Canada Shipping Act was about to be considered by parliament, several organizations such as the St. Lawrence river pilots association and others submitted briefs, copies of which were furnished to hon. members, urging the government to consider the safety factor in the seaway in the light of greatly increased traffic advocating compulsory pilotage. These submissions have no

Canada Shipping Act
doubt been studied and every suggestion considered carefully by the government. The reason for delaying any action at that time, according to the statement of the minister, was because similar legislation was being studied by the United States congress. Our government decided to wait and to introduce amendments to the act which would correspond to changes approved by the United States congress, and that is what appears to be the case now.
This concern over pilotage is shared by the board of marine underwriters. It appears now that a compromise has been adopted to the effect that a pilot is required to be on duty in the narrow channels, as outlined by the minister a moment ago, and in congested areas but not on the long stretches of open water.
With regard to foreign ships, there is an objection to the granting of a B licence to masters and officers of these ships, some of which may present a distinct hazard especially if there happens to be a language barrier. The United States have solved their pilotage problem. Their solution is to leave it to the president to decide what parts of the lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway within the territorial waters of the United States require the use of pilots on foreign ships. I am not suggesting that the minister should assume the power to make these decisions. As pilots would be required in the narrow waters and not on the open lakes, a special licence granted to a ship's captain certifying that he is familiar with the rules of navigation on the great lakes should be sufficient.
Suggestions have been made that Canada should enact legislation to govern the movement of trade within Canadian waters. This idea is a good one because British and United States ships move bulk and general cargo between one Canadian port to another. Canadian ships cannot go to the lakehead, pick up a cargo and deliver it to any other port in the United States, but a United States registered ship can go to the lakehead', pick up a cargo and deliver it to any port in Canada. If that is so, then I submit that there are other amendments to this act which would be quite in order.
It is generally conceded that the greater proportion of world commerce is still being carried by sea going ships. Notwithstanding all other means of modern transportation, nothing can touch them in efficiency, low costs and dependability. Canada owes a great deal to the power of the merchant marine in the development of natural resources, and our industries thrive and prosper because millions of tons of goods and materials move in and out of Canadian ports every year.
[Mr. Badanai.l
We are fortunate in having a few shipping companies operating under Canadian registry whose owners happily are men of patriotism, vision and faith and courage in the future of our country. These men were chiefly responsible for retaining for Canada a semblance of a national merchant marine. One of these companies is the Paterson Steamship Lines which was founded by Senator N. M. Paterson with its head office Fort William.

A few moments ago I was trying to point out the importance of having a Canadian merchant marine. The Canadian
Supply-Transport
great lakes shipping industry could provide the foundation upon which to build an international commercial fleet worthy of a major trading nation. During the war, Canada built training and fighting ships. Some of these were built at the Port Arthur shipbuilding yard which at present is not doing much. However, this yard has the experience in both management and personnel to build ships for any purpose. It is regrettable that many ships of Canadian registry were built in foreign shipyards and that many more are being built abroad. The federal government could bolster dwindling employment in Canadian shipyards by encouraging shipbuilding in every possible way.
The Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing association in one of its letters had this to say, and I quote:
Building ships or manufacturing goods in Canada benefits the national economy as a whole. A large percentage of the price of a ship, probably 40 per cent, finds its way into public treasuries as taxes on income, on profits, on real estate, on the sale of goods bought with the incomes created by the total operations in the building of a ship in Canada. In the case of a foreign-built ship, all such taxes go to another country.
Other considerations which apply particularly to shipbuilding are:
1.	Employment: Shipbuilding not only provides jobs for highly skilled men in the shipyards but also provides jobs for a great variety of types of labour in widely dispersed small communities and big cities of Canada where mines, mills, and manufacturing plants, producing ships' components and materials, are located.
2.	Security: Ships are of vital importance to Canada. A country which lives on its ability to transport goods by water cannot afford to depend on other countries for ships. In emergencies they may not be available. Canada needs its own shipbuilding industry to maintain its economic independence and political sovereignty just as much as it needs its own defence forces. Indeed its navy could not operate in troubled times without Canadian shipyards.
I commend those sentiments to the minister and to the government. We are subsidizing wheat growers, hog producers, egg producers, coal mines, gold mines and railways; why not give a little help to the shipbuilding industry? Why not re-establish the Canadian merchant marine which was allowed to disappear so ingloriously a couple of years ago? Whatever the circumstances surrounding the disposal of those ships, the action taken at that time has not added to the stature of our nation. If a mistake was made-and I submit that the sale of those eight ships to Cuba was a mistake-let us admit it and renew our efforts with the vigour which is the characteristic of everything Canadian.
I realize that enthusiasm for the idea of a subsidized merchant fleet would probably be challenged on the ground that it would result in additional taxes, but I submit that the benefits resulting from a policy of assistance

Supp ly-Transport
to shipbuilding and the development of a merchant fleet would more than offset the cost of such a program.
Not long ago I saw a report in a newspaper to the effect that Greece intends to spend more than $10 million to build a fleet of six freighters for the great lakes-Mediterranean trade. This means that the Hellenic lines will be entering the St. Lawrence seaway for the first time. These ships will bear cargoes to and from such ports as Naples, Istanbul and Beirut, and they are expected to be put into service by the summer of 1961.
Where will these freighters be built? Not in Canada. Our exports and imports will be carried through the great lakes by vessels of other countries.
Canada builds fewer ships than Finland. Our deep-sea fleet which ten years ago numbered some 200 vessels, is now less than a dozen and these are mainly oil tankers sailing between the United States and Canadian ports.
Our shores front on three great oceans, the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic. I especially want to underline the reference to the Arctic ocean. If the Prime Minister's vision ever comes to fruition and we witness an increased development of the north the Arctic ocean will become a great sea lane. In addition we have the great lakes system which in itself could be classed as another ocean.
Despite all this other nations build ships for us. Other nations operate ships for us. All this is true because we say we cannot possibly afford to build and operate ships ourselves. Then we wonder why we have so many unemployed. The time has surely come to sound a clarion call for the reconstruction and expansion of a national merchant marine. I commend the suggestion to the minister and to the government. They have the power to initiate a movement to bring back our merchant marine and establish our nation in the forefront of seafaring nations of the world. We are the third largest trading nation of the world but so far as shipping is concerned our position is not much superior to that of Switzerland. I sincerely trust that the government will take action as quickly as possible.
I feel strongly about this, Mr. Chairman, because as Canadians we are often prone to boast of our national resources. We boast about what we have under the ground and above it but we say little about the exploitation of what we have in our own country for the benefit of Canadians and for the benefit of those who will come to our shores

in the years ahead. I commend to the government consideration of this great challenge that faces us from coast to coast.
I know that objections will be raised. Some will say that this is all nonsense and that it would cost millions of dollars. It probably would represent a large expenditure but it would be worth it. It would be a Canadian enterprise of which we would be proud and in years to come we could look back upon it as something worth while. Let this 24th parliament take action.

Mr. Chairman, I should like the minister to comment as to what is the attitude of the government toward the policies now being followed by the railroads with respect to curtailing important services at an exceedingly rapid rate and discharging in large numbers men who have had many years' service, thus causing untold hardship to employees of long standing. I should like to know what is the attitude of this government Is it one of saying that the railroads' business is their own, we do not concern ourselves with the policies of either of the railways, if they lay off men with 25 or 30 years of service and put them out on the street and these men are unable to obtain a pension it is no concern of ours; or does the government believe this is a serious matter? If so, what is the attitude of the minister and of the government in respect to this situation?
Already this session I have mentioned the lay-offs that took place at Moncton and those that took place at London because of the pending transfer of the Canadian National Railways car shops from that city. The minister and the government seemed to take the attitude that this is really no concern of the Department of Transport or the government, that it is purely a question of C.N.R. or C.P.R. policy. The minister and the government appear to take the position that they are above and aloof from these situations.
I have frequently travelled by railroad across Canada. I am absolutely appalled by the number of railway employees who have sat with me and told me the same story. Although they have had 20, 25 or 30 years' service they are in danger of being laid off. They tell me that some of their fellow workers in similar occupations have already been laid off and that there seems to be no concern for their future on the part of the minister, the government or the railway companies.
I believe in progress and I believe that railways must be run on a business like basis. At the same time I do not think profits should come so far above the question of the

welfare and livelihood of people whose whole working lives have been devoted to railway service. The railroads today seem to be bent on a policy of curtailing many of the services provided in the past and this is being done as rapidly as possible. Not only are they hurting their own employees of long standing for whom they apparently have no concern whatever but in my opinion they are unduly curtailing services in many parts of Canada. They are curtailing passenger service on all but the main lines and this is being done even on some of the important lines. They appear determined to curtail passenger service even further. They are closing railway stations all across the country on a large scale. Every time a station is closed railway revenues fall off, the communities affected have fewer services and more communities are placed in a difficult position with respect to maintaining their normal operation.
Sectionmen are being laid off. Sections are being combined with fewer men. I am wondering if this does not contribute to the great increase of railway accidents? Perhaps a lack of proper maintenance help has contributed to the increased number of accidents.
The services I have mentioned are being curtailed all across Canada. Once a station has been closed for a few years the next move by the company is to remove the caretaker engaged to provide minimum services at that point.
There has been a great deal of discussion as to whether or not the Crowsnest pass rates are in jeopardy. I do not think they are. I do not think that all the propaganda that can be commanded by the C.N.R. or C.P.R. against the rates will result in moving any public minded person who has a knowledge both of this country and its railways or in moving this or any other government to dispense with the Crowsnest pass rates. If I had been making these remarks a week or so ago I would have said the same thing. In the light of recent political events in two provinces I am even more certain that this government will have nothing whatever to do with any abandonment of the Crowsnest pass rates.
I am pleased that I have that conviction because I think the Crowsnest pass rates in this country were part and parcel of an agreement of long standing. One part of the agreement had to do with these particular rates, but another part of the agreement gave very substantial advantages to the railways of this country. What I an wondering is whether there is some kind of back room agreement whereby the railway companies will not be allowed to get higher freight rates on grain but where, in return for having
Supply-Transport
to accept the Crowsnest pass rates in the future, they will be given the green light for a further and an even more rapid curtailment of railway services. I think this is what is happening. I think that for all practical purposes today the board of transport commissioners have shut their eyes to the public demand that minimum services be maintained. For all practical purposes today the board of transport commissioners are acting purely and simply as agents of the railway companies of this country and are doing their bidding when it comes to curtailment of services, the closing of stations and the reduction of train services of all kinds.
This is being pushed even a step farther. Now we see a number of instances where the railway companies are applying to the board of transport commissioners for permission to abandon railway lines. Then they will be pulling up the tracks. As a matter of fact, they are already pulling up one set -that is, the C.P.R.-of the double tracks between Moose Jaw and Swift Current. They argue that the double trackage is not needed there. The railways are determined to pull up a large part of the railway branch lines in this country. 1 do not think it is confined to any one area, but certainly the railways are bent and determined on tearing up a very substantial mileage of trackage on the prairies and on the abandonment of a very large number of branch lines.
The people of this country have an economic interest in the maintenance of the Crowsnest pass rates. They need to watch that what is being saved on the one hand by the maintenance of the Crowsnest pass rates is not lost on the other by the abandonment of railway lines. I notice that the minister thinks this is all very amusing, but it is not amusing for the people to have their railway lines abandoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speechtext: I have paid plenty of attention; I am listening very attentively.

This is a very serious matter to the producers and to the communities that are being faced with an abandonment of their railway lines, perhaps the tearing up of railway lines and the complete disintegration of ther communities.
The producers of western Canada are very much concerned that the Crowsnest pass rates be maintained, but it will be of little advantage if in the maintenance of those rates the railway lines going to their marketing points in many instances are removed so that the saving, whatever it may be, of 10 cents or 15 cents a bushel that is brought about by the maintenance of the Crowsnest pass rates -and nobody knows what the saving is because nobody knows what the railways would get if the board of transport commissioners and the government decided that those rates were not to be maintained-is eaten up by a loss of the trackage to their local marketing points, and they are forced to haul their products a much longer distance. If a person who has been accustomed to hauling his grain a distance of six or eight miles is forced by the subsequent abandonment of railway lines to haul his grain 15 or 20 miles he will find there is a very substantial increase in his costs.
I would ask the minister to tell the committee what attention the government gives to the necessity of the maintenance of railway services in this country, and whether the government has given any thought whatsoever to the policies of the railway companies in endeavouring to have branch lines abandoned in the country. I would ask the minister also to tell the committee whether the government has given any consideration to the plight of the thousands of railway workers who are being displaced, and whether any study is going on in the department of the minister, or in the Department of Labour, on the plight of those people and what their job opportunities may be in the future. I do not think it is in keeping with a modern society that we should cast off on the labour market after 25 or 30 years of diligent service those people who have been employees of the railway companies and have
[Mr. Argued
provided excellent service to the people of this country without any consideration whatsoever for their future.
The firemen, because of a very strong union, have been able to make an agreement which to some extent at any rate has protected the livelihood of men in that occupation. As I understand it, the agreement they now have does not prevent modernization. It merely means that the people who are in that occupation at the present time cannot be summarily dismissed without any consideration for their future. I do not know that that is the kind of pattern that could or should be applied to other sections of the railways, but I do feel that the railways of this country have some obligation to employees who have invested their lives in the occupation of railroading. I think the government should tell this committee very frankly what consideration it has given to the very serious situation in which many railroaders now find themselves, and also what consideration the government is giving to the maintenance of a minimum railway service in this country.
As I now see it, in the headlong rush toward so-called modernization with the sole objective of making profits both the employees of the railway companies and the public as a whole are likely to suffer. Last night I was at the new Ottawa airport terminal building and as a Canadian I was exceedingly proud of this magnificent building. It has been placed there because governments of this country have believed it was a good investment. The air lines are able to make use of the services provided by this very substantial public investment.
The only reason I point this out is to say that in the field of transportation there must be a yardstick applied which is not purely the yardstick of profit. There must be a yardstick applied which takes into account the well-being and welfare of the employees and the welfare of and services available to the general public.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Could I answer the hon. member as we go along? I should like to answer some of the comments he has made. The hon. member for Assiniboia brought up the question of the relationship between the government and the management of the railway in the day to day management of the affairs of the railway. I should like to point out to him something which I feel sure he knows. Many years ago parliament decided that the management of the C.N.R. should be 100 per cent in the hands of the railway management. The act passed at that time specifically prohibited the government from interfering in the day to day management of the railway. That is the law.

As to the concern of the government with regard to the service provided by Canadian National Railways, I want to assure the hon. member that the government is very much interested in and concerned about the service that the C.N.R. provides to the people of Canada. It is a vital service and the government is very much concerned about it. It pays a great deal of attention to it and discusses it with the management.
This government and this ministry are also very vitally concerned about lay-offs, any lay-offs. As I have pointed out to the house on many occasions, I and the government are very much disturbed at even one lay-off. It is a dreadful thing when even one man has to be deprived of a job. We feel the situation very sincerely and acutely because not only is the man deprived of employment but there is also an effect on his morale and that of his family. We understand that. We have talked over this matter many times with the management of the C.N.R. They also feel the same way about it and they have assured me over and over and over again on the many occasions I have discussed the matter with them that they do everything possible to keep the employee on the job as long as he possibly can be employed, as long as there is work for him to do. But they have pointed out that because of changes in the nature of the work, because of technological improvements and things of that kind they simply cannot employ a man to do nothing when there is literally no work for him to do.
I feel sure the hon. member will agree that that it is sensible, undesirable though it is that the man should be without a job. When it becomes necessary to deprive men of work because there is no work for them to do the management have assured me that they take every possible step to see that these people are put in some other job in every possible case. I have discussed these matters on many occasions with the management and they have assured me, and I believe them, that this is so. The men concerned with management with whom I have talked are sincere men who mean what they say.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great care to what has been said by the hon. member for Fort William in his discussion of ship construction, navigation and a merchant marine for Canada, and I find myself in agreement with what he had to say. I have also listened carefully to what was said by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I must tell the Minister of Transport that I am sure that he, like all other members of the house, must of necessity feel badly when men employed by Canadian National Railways are laid off, and the Canadian Pacific 79951-0-344

railway too for that matter. But feeling badly about a situation does not remedy it. It is not enough for the minister to say what he has said this evening and has repeated on a number of other occasions, that he is convinced in his own mind that Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian Pacific railway for that matter, do not lay off men unless they are convinced there is no further work for them. That may be so but that does not help the situation.
Notwithstanding that, I understand the fact is that some 7,000 or 8,000 men have been laid off by Canadian National Railways. I have on my desk a letter that reached me during the course of last week from certain interests indicating that there are many layoffs on the Canadian Pacific railway. While I know that the minister is not responsible for the Canadian Pacific railway, nevertheless I also know that he is interested in railway operations from one end of the country to the other, and today the operations of railways are perhaps more difficult not only in Canada but in the United States than they have been in many years.
While I find myself in general agreement with what was said by the hon. member for Assiniboia with respect to lay-offs on the railways, I must say that I cannot support his rather severe criticism of the board of transport commissioners. I do not believe that the board of transport commissioners is an instrument or tool of Canadian National Railways Or any other railway. The board of transport commissioners was established by act of parliament and they put into effect the sections of the Railway Act under which the railways make applications. If we in this parliament want to meet the situation which the hon. member for Assiniboia has raised, and there is a great deal to be said for what he has advanced; if we want to change the position we must change the act because as the law now stands Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific railway have the right under the act to proceed as they do.
With the approval of the board.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member was not listening to me. He was talking to his friends.
That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I said that the board' of transport commissioners is bound by the Railway Act and must apply the Railway Act when an application is made, unfortunate as this may be. I know that when I held the position now held by the Minister of Transport a similar situation occurred in my own riding and there was absolutely nothing I

Supply-Transport
could do about it except to explain the position to those affected thereby. I am talking now about the New York Central railway which ran from one end of my former riding of Stormont to the other. The board of transport commissioners was bound by the Railway Act. Let the hon. member not misunderstand me. I am sympathetic to those people who live along a railway line and find themselves deprived of railway services but I think the remedy perhaps lies in another direction by way of amendment to the act.
However, I did not rise for that purpose but for another. It may be that the minister may not like the purpose of this discussion, but nevertheless I hope he will listen to it because I intend to discuss this matter with the sole object of being constructive in the criticism I have to offer of the minister, his officials and those of the Department of Public Works.
I speak now of the joint team which has been established by the two departments in connection with port facilities along the St. Lawrence. The minister may find this annoying, but even if he does smile I will not be offended because I know that on occasions I have found myself in the same circumstances as the minister does.
I made a motion many weeks ago asking for the production in this house of documents which the minister had discussed, namely the 29 reports that were made on ports extending from the lower St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec to, I believe, within the metropolitan area of Toronto at Oshawa. This motion was defeated. The government, with its huge majority, voted it down. I want to deal with the manner in which that was done as compared with what was done in former years.
The minister, in the discussion in the house and in the committee, ridiculed the idea of an economic survey of the St. Lawrence seaway as I had suggested. I hold in my hand a document prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce, economic research division, in January, 1951 on the effect of the St. Lawrence seaway upon the Canadian economy. This is a very important and fairly lengthy document containing 144 pages and it deals, amongst other things, with the case for the St. Lawrence seaway; the case for the St. Lawrence power development; the potential water traffic upon the seaway; the minimum estimate of water benefits; the capital costs and carrying charges; and last, but not least, about 25 pages dealing with the effect upon regional and special economic interests of Canada, particularly the prairie provinces, Ontario, Quebec, Newfoundland, the mari-times and British Columbia, Canadian ports,
[Mr. Chevrier.J
Canadian railways, lake shipping and shipbuilding. This document is a public document which anyone can obtain and it was made public by the then minister of trade and commerce.
When I made the motion in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines in 1958, I believe two years ago, asking that the St. Lawrence seaway authority undertake an economic survey of the effect of the seaway upon the various regions of Canada, I felt that there should be an up-to-date document similar to this which would indicate to the various regions of Canada the beneficial or adverse, if any, effects of this project upon the economy of our country. The committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines voted unanimously in its recommendation for the adoption of that economic survey. The minister saw fit not to accede to this recommendation and I believe in the course of his statement, either in the committee or in the house, he said he thought that it was ridiculous.
I want to say that I believe the team which the minister has set up may be a good thing in individual cases but it is not what is required when one must consider the overall position of the various ports. You cannot have a study of a local situation unless you know what the effect of this power and navigation project, both in Ontario and Quebec, is likely to be upon the rest of Canada. You cannot know that unless a statement of its effect, such as this one, is brought up to date or a new one, having regard to new circumstances, is prepared. It seemed to me at that time that that was essential,' and I believe that what has happened since has proved that what I suggested to the committee was right.
The team which was established by the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport has taken officials in the Department of Transport and in the Department of Public Works to do what? They have considered a plan in each individual port, 29 of which have been mentioned, and the information upon which was refused to the House of Commons. Do you know what this team does? Notwithstanding the fact that it considers information from both departments, there is no one from the St. Lawrence seaway authority on this team of experts. How in the world, I ask the minister and the government, is this team going to do the kind of job that is expected of it if it does not get information from those who possess it, namely the St. Lawrence seaway authority who in turn have the information possessed by the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation of the United States? I said earlier that this information in the United States is being

compiled. There should be a representative from the seaway authority on this team.
I hold in my hand now a study made by the New York Central railway system, showing industrial sites all along the United States side of the seaway from Rooseveltown, New York, to Oswego, New York. There is a map of each port; there is a description of the facilities; there is the cost and value of the land; there is the assessment, the taxation, the water rates, everything is contained in this study with respect to even the smallest of these sites. Has the Department of Transport or the Department of Public Works published anything of this nature? If they have, we have not been able to see it.
I think the government must begin now to try to find secondary industries which will establish themselves along both shores of the St. Lawrence seaway. I use that expression with regard to Canada and not with regard to the United States. By "both shores", I mean both the north and south shore of the lower St. Lawrence as well as the north shore of the upper St. Lawrence. I would be glad to send this document over to the minister so that he may see how well it has been prepared. Copies of this document have been sent to thousands of industrial plants not only in the United States but on the continent of Europe, with the result that secondary industry is establishing itself on the United States side of the line but not on the Canadian side.
Here at Rooseveltown in New York state and alongside of it there are two large industries which have established themselves there. One is Reynolds Aluminum and the other is Chevrolet branch of General Motors. I believe they employ about 7,000 people between them. It seems to me that some consideration should be given by the government to what has been done on the other side of the line.
