speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not disagree with the hon. member, but I want to make clear to the committee that he is the one who had the opportunity during a long period of time when he had responsibilities to do something about that which he is now discussing.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Oh, no. When I was in the seaway authority, the job of the authority was to build a channel 27 feet in depth from Montreal to the foot of lake Erie and to expropriate land for that purpose. The second job was to establish tolls, not to establish industry. That is not the job of the St. Lawrence seaway at all; that is the job of the government as a whole, and the government of this country is not doing a thing to establish secondary industry along the seaway.
But I do not want to get away from what I intended to say. I want to come now to another public document, a document prepared by Canadian National Railways dealing with the proposed St. Lawrence deep waterways project affecting the city of Cornwall and the surrounding country. Here in my hand is a report by Canadian National Railways which has also been made public. It contains a series of maps and some 70 or 80 pages of material on the area. The point I am trying to make is that these reports were made public to the municipality. We in this committee and those ports which are affected know all about these plans but we cannot find out a thing in so far as the plans of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport are concerned.
The other evening we discussed this matter in the house, and the purpose of my rising to discuss it now is that I think the ports of Seven Islands, Baie Comeau, the new port which is being established upstream from Seven Islands and Rimouski. Matane and all those ports in the province of Quebec not under the national harbours board; Cornwall, Brockville, and I believe Belleville,

Supply-Transport
have all been studied, from Dorion right up to Oshawa. I think the committee should get some idea what the officials have in mind. The hon. member for Essex East mentioned Windsor and Sarnia and the other ports which were mentioned by the minister during the course of his discussions.
I do not think these men are able to tell us what is likely to happen in one particular area, for example Cornwall, unless there is an over-all plan and unless someone has studied the effect of this power and navigation project upon the various regions of Canada. Have they studied the McGill report on metropolitan Montreal? Have they studied the effect of the seaway upon grain, perhaps one of the finest reports which have been made on the subject by the Chicago board of trade in conjunction with the University of Indiana? Have they studied this report of Canadian National Railways to which I have referred and which deals with the whole international section but more particularly with Cornwall? If they have not, they should.
What have they come down with? They have come down with a report which involves an expenditure of $80,000 in the city of Cornwall. Let me tell the minister what this team actually did when they went to the city of Cornwall. They went to the city of Cornwall and they examined the west end and came to the conclusion that that is where the wharf facilities should go. It was suggested to them that they should look at the facilities that existed opposite the city of Cornwall and they said "No". This is what I want to bring to the attention of the minister. They said, "Oh, no, the water is too swift there; you could not think of establishing a wharf there because the velocity is about eight feet per second". These experts of the Departments of Transport and Public Works did not even know that the St. Lawrence seaway was carrying on works to broaden the cross-sectional area and reduce the velocity of the water from eight to less than four feet per second in order to establish the entrance to a canal, a future canal with 27-foot facilities on the Canadian side of the line.
It was not until after that had been pointed out to their attention that they went back there. And what did they do? They changed their plans from the west end of Cornwall and they went down to the east end and said, "Here is a place which we think is ideal". It is not hard to see when one looks at the map included in the Canadian National Railways report that the amount of water varies in depth all along the eastern front of Cornwall extending from Grays creek to

Courtaulds on the west. The map indicates the water is at every point greater than 27 feet in depth. When you get close to this wharf which has been recommended by the team for extension you have 31 feet, 35 feet and 41 feet. So that a small extension only of the wharf will reach deep water.
I am not complaining about the decision. The decision is probably a good one but it should have been taken twelve months earlier. Furthermore the decision to spend $80,000 is not nearly enough. Far more than that is required in this particular instance, and I add-and I emphasize this to those who sit on the other side of the house-that if the government really wants to deal with the cyclical and the technological unemployment situation in Canada it must of necessity do something toward the establishment of secondary industry. This is the time because here you have in the first year of the seaway six million tons of traffic coming from overseas as compared with less than one million tons prior to the opening of the seaway last year.
Where is that six million tons going to go? It is the business and the duty not so much of this committee to ascertain that but of a committee which would study the effect upon Canada as a whole then allow the team that the minister speaks of with the information that it has in hand to come forward and deal with a particular and a local situation.
Then there is the tremendous amount of domestic traffic. Who would have thought four or five years ago that the traffic on the St. Lawrence canals would amount to 20 million tons and on the Welland canal to 27 million tons? The figures which the minister's department has published for 1960 up until May indicate now a new trend which is a trend away from the smaller ship in favour of the larger ship, which means that there should be greater and greater tonnage. That means tonnage not only for domestic traffic but also, I presume, for ocean traffic. That is why I think that a great deal more can be done for the establishment of secondary industry in this whole great lakes-St. Lawrence basin from the lower St. Lawrence right up to the head of the lakes than is being done now.
I said earlier that the United States is giving consideration to this, and I do not think we are doing enough. I am not saying that the team is incompetent. Certainly I would not make a statement such as that. But I do not think the team which the minister has set up is the kind of team required to do the job.
How would the hon. gentleman change it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I said earlier-if the hon. member had been here he would know- that the report made in 1951 by the economics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce should be brought up to date. That in effect was the recommendation I made in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines which was approved unanimously but which the minister thought should not be put into effect. I will not use the term which he used, because I do not want to be involved in an argument with the hon. gentleman so late in the evening. In any event, the minister could not find himself able to give favourable consideration to the recommendation. If a report of that kind which was made public in 1951, and which was an extremely well prepared document, were prepared with reference to the new situation-because when that report was drafted it was not possible to envisage the conditions as they were found in 1956 and 1957, and even today-if a report such as this was given to parliament, plus the work done by the team established by the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works, I think you would have great co-ordination and liaison one with another. As it is, I do not think we have that, and I hope the minister will take these remarks which I have made in good part, because they are meant to be constructive and are not offered in any other way.

I should like to deal with a subject which has been causing me and I am sure a number of other Canadians a great deal of concern, that is, the very inefficient transport system we have developed across the country. I am not saying this in criticism of the present minister. I think this is a situation which has developed from coast to coast largely without our being conscious of it. Year after year we have to subsidize our railway systems to an increasing extent. In addition to subsidizing the railways as such, we subsidize as individuals who have to travel on the railways; we subsidize fares because the fares have been increasing all the time, and we subsidize meals because the price of meals has been going up all the time until one has to pay about three times as much on a train as what a comparable or better meal would cost elsewhere. We subsidize freight, we subsidize express, we subsidize everything.
Not long ago I was going to visit my brother in the province of Quebec. I can recall that when I was a lad one of the big events of the day was going down to meet the train when it came through. I wanted to stop at Scotstown, but in order to meet this particular train my brother would have to go
Supply-Transport
either to Megantic, 40 miles away, or to Sherbrooke, 40 miles in the other direction, because the train does not stop at Scotstown any longer. That, when I come to think of it, is another kind of subsidy. It is little wonder that more and more people are turning to air travel where one does not have to pay three times as much as a meal would normally cost; the meal is provided free, and it is served by an attractive hostess in the bargain. If people do not fly, they go back to the highways and drive, to avoid the inconvenience which they might otherwise encounter. This in turn means that trains are running empty and the subsidy has to be increased.
The railways have made every effort to economize. They have used every device of modern technique and automation to this end. They have even, in my opinion, carried this process to extremes, because as some hon. members have mentioned the length of track allotted to repair gangs has been increased, while the number of men at work has been cut down. More and more wrecks have resulted, but, thank heavens, there has been so far no great loss of life. Any of us who travel a great deal on the railways have noticed that the roads are getting rougher and rougher all the time; it has come to the point on some tracks where it is best to tie yourself in the bunk if you do not want to end up on the floor.
Because of considerations such as I have mentioned people are shipping their freight and express to an increasing extent by road transport. Road transportation is taking over much of the work which was formerly done by the railways. What do we do in this respect? Again we subsidize. We subsidize the transportation interests by building the roads over which their vehicles travel, whereas the railways have to build and maintain their own roads. Thus motor transport is increasing the difficulties of the railways and at the same time it is pounding our highways to pieces and increasing our highway costs; highways which would last for years if travelled only by private motor traffic are being broken up in a year or two by these huge vehicles.
With this increased traffic by both passenger and transport vehicles problems such as the question of safety at level crossings are bound to arise. We have reached the stage where all level crossings will have to be abolished. We seldom hear of a week end passing without one or more fatal accidents caused by a motor vehicle colliding with a train at a level crossing.
May I call it ten o'clock?

speechtext: May I inquire what the leader of the house intends to do tomorrow and for the rest of the week, if possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
For tomorrow we have three legislative items. We shall begin with Bill No. S-35, an act respecting the international boundary commission, followed by a resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport dealing with the Freight Rates Reduction Act. The third item is the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister concerning the setting up of a department of forestry.
It may be we shall complete those three items tomorrow, making similar progress to that we have made today. If so, I would ask the indulgence of the house to proceed with the estimates of the Department of Transport. On Wednesday, if the estimates
of the department are not concluded, we shall carry on with those estimates. Then we have the estimates of the departments of justice and fisheries which by arrangement with hon. gentlemen opposite we can take in whatever order is satisfactory.
Friday being Dominion day I am not sure what the house will want to do on this occasion but last year the house met at eleven o'clock and rose at one. That may be what will be done this year as well. In any case on Friday we will start with the bill which the Prime Minister will introduce, an act for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms and we will continue the debate on that subject matter the following week.
It being two minutes after ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
